📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, early Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a new space exploration milestone: The probe, which released in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth.

The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.

Recent findings suggest that the growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe. But with Voyager 1 still collecting data with two of its science instruments, which are expected to stay powered up into the 2030s, NASA scientists say one thing is certain: The spacecraft isn't done surprising us.

"What Voyager has taught me is to expect the unexpected," Linda Spilker, who joined the Voyager team in 1977 and is the mission's current project scientist, told Live Science in an interview. "So many times the ideas and theories we had, Voyager was able to prove them wrong.".

Here, we look back at some of Voyager 1's most groundbreaking discoveries, told through its incredible photos.

NASA's Voyager 1 probe launches atop a Titan/Centaur-6 launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

In a recent development, NASA's Voyager 2 probe debuted before Voyager 1, on Aug. 20, 1977. Voyager 1 took off a few weeks later, on Sept. 5. (The two spacecraft took slightly different routes through the solar system, allowing Voyager 1 to reach interstellar space first after a gravity boost from Jupiter and Saturn.).

Spilker, who joined NASA right out of college, attended the historic Voyager 2 launch and recalls "that feeling of watching the rocket lift up off the launchpad, feeling the roar of those rocket engines and knowing this was a mission going to visit places I'd always been curious about.".

A few weeks after launching, Voyager 1 took this photo of a crescent Earth and moon from 7.25 million miles (11.66 million km) from Earth.

On its way to the outer solar system, Voyager 1 snapped this image of a crescent Earth and its moon, captured in the same frame for the first time ever.

It has been revealed that voyager 1 photographed Jupiter from January to April 1979, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As the spacecraft zoomed closer to the giant planet, it snapped an image every 96 seconds, creating this incredible time-lapse animation of the planet's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of one Earth month.

Sources indicate that the close-up view highlighted that Jupiter is a far more dynamic world than previously thought. But Voyager also made key discoveries about the planet's many moons.

Industry observers note that while passing by the Jovian moon Io, Voyager 1 witnessed an explosion: the first volcanic eruption ever seen beyond Earth. This proved that there were other geologically active worlds in our solar system, opening up entirely new avenues of inquiry and exploration.

A blue eruption on Jupiter's moon Io, the first volcanic eruption seen on another world.

"Going in, we thought that the moons would look a lot like our own moon: ancient dead worlds," Spilker said. "And yet we found out they were very different worlds — like Io with active volcanoes. It was just an incredible change in our thinking.".

By viewing these eruptions, scientists saw parts of Io's surface being changed in real time. "As we got closer [to Io], scientists kept saying the surface is getting younger and younger, because they didn't see any big craters, no medium sized craters, no little craters — until finally parts of its surface are just minutes old," Spilker noted.

A mosaic view of Callisto taken from Voyager 1 photos at a distance of about 250,000 miles (400,000 km).

Some of Voyager's close-up observations also confirmed old theories. For example, Voyager 1's flyby of the moon Callisto in March 1979 revealed vast fields of well-preserved impact craters, proving that Callisto was geologically dead.

Jupiter and its thin ring of dust backlit by the sun in a Voyager 1 image.

A final surprise at Jupiter came when Voyager 1 swooped around the planet's nightside, seeing the gas giant backlit by the sun. This view revealed a thin ring system around the planet, made partly of the dust particles Io spewed into space.

Voyager 1 reached Saturn in November 1980 and made its closest approach to the planet on Nov. 12 of that year. Four days later, the spacecraft took this image of the planet's nightside, showing a broad shadow cast onto the surrounding rings.

According to recent reports, "That is one of my favorite pictures: an outbound image, taken by Voyager looking at [Saturn] in a way you could never see from the Earth," Spilker said, noting that we can only ever see Saturn's sunlit side from our planet. "The rings just look so beautiful shining there, and you can actually see the shadow of Saturn on the rings themselves. It's a really, really special picture.".

In addition to discovering a previously unknown ring, Voyager 1 spotted five fresh moons around Saturn and took close-up photos of several other known satellites.

Voyager 1's closeup view of Titan revealed a dense, hazy atmosphere.

The mission required Voyager to swing by the moon Titan in order to bend the probe's trajectory, sending it away from the solar system's planetary plane and toward a rendezvous with interstellar space. Before that, Voyager 1 revealed Titan's atmosphere to be so hazy that it completely obscured the moon's surface. This revealed that Titan's clogged atmosphere was far denser than those of Earth and Mars.

By 1990, Voyager 1 was so far from the planetary plane that our solar system's planets looked like little more than specks of light. But before turning off its camera for good, Voyager 1 looked back at our cosmic neighborhood and took some of the most iconic space photos of all time.

Industry observers note that in a series of 64 images taken from roughly 40 times Earth's distance from the sun, Voyager snapped its solar system "family portrait," a mosaic of images capturing six planets together for the first time. The portrait included views of Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Frames from Voyager 1's family portrait showing Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

The image of Earth from this collection is famously known as the "Pale Blue Dot.".

"We took the pictures of the planets in color, and that one is especially one of my favorites," Spilker stated. "There's Earth captured in a sunbeam. A tiny world less than a pixel in size representing all the life that we know in our solar system — just a very special image reminding us just how special and precious our planet is.".

Earth appears as a pale blue dot in this iconic Voyager 1 image.

Voyager 1 turned off its camera immediately after taking these images, concluding its role as the greatest tourist in the history of our solar system. In 2012, Voyager 1 passed beyond the heliopause — the boundary where the sun's radiation gives way to the interstellar medium — becoming the first interstellar spacecraft in history.

Industry observers note that voyager 2 crossed the same boundary in 2018 and is expected to reach its own light-day in 2035. In the meantime, several science instruments remain active on both probes, allowing them to measure the strange and mysterious environment between stars.

Even way out there, the probes are still detecting whispers of the sun's power.

Sources indicate that "We are still seeing effects from the sun that come out, hit the heliopause, and send shocks and pressure fronts out into the interstellar medium," Spilker stated. "I wonder where we will finally reach the point where the sun doesn't influence what we're seeing, and we're in the pristine interstellar medium — and I hope that happens while Voyager 1 is still operating.".

Sources indicate that brandon is the space / physics editor at Live Science. With more than 20 years of editorial experience, his writing has appeared in The Washington Post, Reader's Digest, CBS.com, the Richard Dawkins Foundation website and other outlets. He holds a bachelor's degree in creative writing from the University of Arizona, with minors in journalism and media arts. His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.

  • The move clears the way for Senate Ethics Chairman James Lankford, R-Okla., to use his seniority to ascend to ranking Republican on the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which Paul at the moment chairs, and touches off several other shifts at the top of other committees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., leaves the Senate Republicans’ lunch in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

In a recent development, sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., announced Wednesday he prepares to serve as the top Republican on the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee when Democrats take control of Congress next year.

The move clears the way for Senate Ethics Chairman James Lankford, R-Okla., to use his seniority to ascend to ranking Republican on the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which Paul at the moment chairs, and touches off several other shifts at the top of other committees.

Recent findings suggest that the move fit in with Sen. Lisa Murkowski’s bid to use her seniority to succeed Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, as top Republican on the Appropriations panel. If Paul did not go to the top spot on HELP, Murkowski, R-Alaska, would be next in line for that committee in the next Congress.

Murkowski is second in seniority on Appropriations to Collins, who was defeated for reelection. But she faces a potential challenge from Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., who is next in line behind her.

Paul noted in a press release that he plans to bring the same approach to the HELP Committee as he did as chairman of Homeland, where he said he “challenged entrenched bureaucracies, forced federal officials to answer for their actions, and pulled back the curtain on what Washington tried to keep hidden.”.

He cited calling Dr. Anthony Fauci before the committee to probe the former federal health official’s role in pandemic-related shutdowns and the origin of the COVID-19 virus, and releasing thousands of pages of pandemic-related documents. The panel voted in August to hold Fauci in criminal contempt of Congress for declining to answer questions about the pandemic during a highly charged hearing.

Related: Fauci could face criminal contempt charge following panel vote.

Paul, an ophthalmologist, mentioned at HELP he will “stand against efforts to put Washington between Americans and their doctors, their children’s schools, and their paychecks.” He predicted “a rush toward socialism unlike anything we have seen” when the Democrat-controlled Congress convenes in January.

According to recent reports, lankford, in a separate statement, confirmed his interest in becoming the ranking member of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. In many areas, he said, the panel can work in a bipartisan manner, and over the past decade he “worked across the aisle to improve emergency communications in federal buildings, strengthen the United States Postal Service, increase federal cybersecurity preparedness, government transparency, and the use of artificial intelligence.”.

In a recent development, but he added that his job also would be to “push back on a [Democratic] majority that goes too far . . . Oversight is responsible, but obstruction is unacceptable.”.

In a recent development, lankford stated he would work together with the likely committee chair, Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., “when we can agree and be a fierce opposition if there is an attempt to undercut our nation’s security.”.

Tech Report: 7 Simple Steps for Winterizing Your Lawn Mower

📅 16 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1325 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Sources indicate that somehow the end of the year is upon us and mowing season is winding down.
  • Recent findings suggest that winterizing is especially crucial for gas-powered mowers, which have engines that need fuel, oil, and an air filter to run properly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that somehow the end of the year is upon us and mowing season is winding down. And while you should still be mowing your lawn until the first hard frost hits, soon it’ll be time to retire it for the winter, and you get to give that chore a rest for a bit. But you can’t just store the mower in the shed and forget about it. To ensure your lawn mower is ready to go next season, you need to winterize it before sending it into hibernation.

Recent findings suggest that winterizing is especially crucial for gas-powered mowers, which have engines that need fuel, oil, and an air filter to run properly. You should do some light maintenance on them before the cold weather arrives. While cordless electric lawn mowers are easier to maintain, there are still a few steps you should take before storing them away.

In a recent development, here are our tips for winterizing any lawn mower so it’s ready to go in the spring. Note that you don’t have to do them in this exact order; for example, you might want to leave fuel stabilization until later in the process, but we wanted to keep it at the top, since it’s one of the most crucial steps.

Sources indicate that prepping your gas-powered lawn mower for winter storage isn’t hard; there are just several things to consider, and if you cover them all, it should only take an hour or so. You will be dealing with engine fluids, however, so choose a work area and clothing that you don’t mind getting dirty.

When left for long periods, gasoline can become “stale,” meaning it evaporates and oxidizes, making it less combustible. It can also create residues that could damage the engine. Also, the ethanol found in most gasoline can break down if left to sit, causing performance issues and attracting water that can cause corrosion (one of the reasons ethanol-free gas is better for lawn mowers).

You can avoid the problems by adding a fuel stabilizer, but if there is any air in the tank, it’s not a perfect solution. Meanwhile, siphoning the gas from the tank is not truly going to remove all of it, so here’s our advice, in steps:.

Sources indicate that not everyone will recommend this method, but we believe that, since a full tank has almost no air in it, there is little space for fuel to evaporate or for condensation to form due to temperature changes. Therefore, you are less likely to encounter problems than if you had drained the tank.

According to recent reports, large gas-powered mowers, such as lawn tractors and zero-turn mowers, typically have a battery to power the starter, lights, and other accessories. Gas walk-behind mowers with an electric start feature will also have a battery. It’s a good idea to remove it for the winter and clean it to remove corrosion on the terminals or battery posts. When performing this task, wear nitrile gloves and eye protection. If your battery has a lot of corrosion, you don't want to remove it in a way that it gets airborne. You can use a solution of water and baking soda to neutralize the corrosion and wipe it off with a rag or microfiber cloth.

In a recent development, most experts recommend replacing your spark plug every year. Changing your spark plug can vary depending on the model of lawn mower you own, so always consult your manual. If you do not feel it’s necessary to replace it, at least remove it to check for any damage. If you see a lot of carbon buildup, rust, or cracks, it’s best to change it.

Drain the oil from the mower after letting it run for 5 minutes—warm oil flows more easily. For walk-behind mowers, this will require you to tip the mower over, so it’s probably better to remove the gas first or at least make sure the gas tank is securely sealed. When tipping the mower, the carburetor and air filter sections should be facing upward to avoid oil contamination—since the oil spout is usually on the opposite side of the carb and filter, you’ll naturally be following this rule anyway. But it’s good advice for when you tip the mower to clean the underside of the deck as well.

It has been revealed that this is pretty easy to do, but it helps to know what the filter is made of. Paper and fiber filters should be replaced. If it’s a foam filter element, you can use water and Dawn dish soap, but make sure to rinse it well and let it air dry completely before reinstalling it.

Sources indicate that you should be cleaning your mower deck throughout the summer, but if not, make a point to do it before storing it; otherwise, the caked-on grass may cause corrosion or attract bugs and vermin. As mentioned above, make sure to tip your mower so that the air box and carburetor are on the high side to avoid fuel contamination.

After you’ve completed the task of cleaning the deck, it’s a good idea to wipe down your engine with a damp cloth, removing any dirt or debris, and dry it with another towel.

In a recent development, the end of the season is a good time to sharpen your mower blade or replace it altogether. You can take it to a lawn mower repair shop to have it done, but if you have a few basic tools, it’s very simple to do it yourself.

The beauty of a cordless mower is that there’s less maintenance you need to perform. But that doesn’t mean there aren’t steps to take before storing it away for winter.

Recent findings suggest that batteries are the lifeblood of a cordless mower, so you need to take care of them. Don’t leave them in the mower over winter, especially if you’re keeping it in an uninsulated shed that sees cold temperatures. Remove your batteries and charge them to between 40 and 60 percent. Check the charge level every two months or so, as lithium-ion batteries lose power over time. Partially recharge the batteries if they dip close to 20 percent or lower.

Store your batteries in a cool, dark place such as a basement or insulated garage (but not near a furnace or heat source). For a riding mower that has a built-in battery you cannot remove, park it in a garage or at least a covered area. If stored in a place that gets below freezing, don’t leave it on a charger or try to recharge it, as some batteries (lithium-ion) should not be charged below 32 degrees Fahrenheit. Get it to a warmer place or wait until a warmer day.

This isn’t much different from how you do it for a gas mower; just be careful if using water to do any cleaning, as this can potentially damage electrical components. Also, be sure to remove the batteries before you do any kind of cleaning on a cordless mower.

Again, this isn’t a different process than a gas mower; just make sure the batteries are removed first to avoid the chance of the mower starting up accidentally.

Industry News: Scott Colom elected Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (765 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov.
  • Industry observers note that democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen.
  • The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov. 4, has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images).

Industry observers note that democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.

Recent findings suggest that colom was leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent — or by just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast — when The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, a little over a week after Election Day. Ty Pinkins, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee who ran as an independent this year, had 2 percent.

In recent days, as absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom had all but declared victory, repeatedly saying that Hyde-Smith had no path to victory.

Industry observers note that “I'll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home,” he posted Monday on social media.

With his victory, Colom joins several other Democrats who flipped seats in deep-red states, including Texas’ James Talarico, Kansas’ Adam Hamilton and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews. Democrats have so far flipped eight Senate seats to win control of the chamber, overcoming a difficult Senate map and giving them their largest majority in the chamber since 2011.

It has been revealed that that majority could expand further if Democrats flip the Senate seat in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

Sources indicate that republicans have dominated Senate elections in Mississippi in recent decades. The last Democrat to be elected senator in the Magnolia State was John C. Stennis, who won his sixth full and final term in 1982. Colom will be the third Black man to serve as a Mississippi senator after Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce during Reconstruction.

While Revels and Bruce, who left office in 1881, were elected by the state Legislature, Colom will be the first Black senator elected directly by voters.

According to recent reports, colom has served as a district attorney for four counties in northeast Mississippi since 2016. President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal district judgeship in 2022, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked his nomination by not returning a so-called blue slip, a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition that lets senators derail district judge nominees in their home states.

Recent findings suggest that senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer said last week that he’d had Colom in his sights for several years as a potential Senate candidate, including for a race against the state’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker.

In a recent development, “I had Scott Colom and his father come to my house, and I served them a nice little brunch or something. I said, ‘You got to run,’” the New York Democrat recalled to MS NOW. “They were smarter than me. This was four years ago. They said, ‘We don’t want to run this time, but we know that Hyde-[Smith], the incumbent, is so weak, we could beat her.’”.

Industry observers note that still, the Mississippi race didn’t capture as much national attention as other Senate contests until the closing weeks of the campaign. A trio of Black senators, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Cory Booker of New Jersey, all campaigned with Colom throughout the summer and fall. Key national figures, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, also stumped for him in October.

Sources indicate that colom’s campaign engaged voters with quirky ads and unconventional forms of outreach, including meeting with people lining up to attend a Trump rally. One ad that went viral played on Hyde Smith saying earlier this year that people had “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about rising beef prices.

According to recent reports, “Pick another protein?” says a man in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”.

Major Democratic outside groups made a late play in the state, with WinSenate, which is affiliated with Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, investing $2.2 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spent $500,000 on a coordinated ad buy late last month.

According to recent reports, the pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund dropped $1.7 million on the race, and Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith on Oct. 26.

Madrid 5-Day Itinerary: A Guide to Culture, Gastronomy, and Local Life

📅 06 May 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2480 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nomadicmatt

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Home to some 3.5 million people, Madrid is the capital of Spain and the country’s largest city.
  • According to recent reports, like Barcelona, Madrid is a city that starts late and goes slow.
  • I’ve been a few times over the years and the city never ceases to amaze me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Home to some 3.5 million people, Madrid is the capital of Spain and the country’s largest city. Though it’s somewhat sprawling, the city boasts stunning architecture, incredible food, and an energetic nightlife that stretches until dawn. Over 10 million people visit the city each year, and the minute you step out to explore, you’ll understand why Madrid is one of Europe’s top destinations.

According to recent reports, like Barcelona, Madrid is a city that starts late and goes slow. It’s a city for night owls, where dinner starts late and the parties even later. But if you can embrace the laid-back pace of life, the slow meals, and the late-night vibes, you’ll have a more authentic visit and uncover the true beating heart of the city’s culture.

I love all my visits to Madrid. I’ve been a few times over the years and the city never ceases to amaze me. The food, the energy, the art (so much art!). Madrid is just cool.

Being such a substantial city, I know it can be easy to feel lost. Where do you start with what you want to do? Where do you go? It took me a few visits to figure it out.

In this post, I’ll help you plan an epic five-day visit to Madrid that will ensure you not only see the main sights but that you also get off the beaten path and see just what makes Madrid so popular — and all without breaking the bank either!

It has been revealed that this first day focuses on a prestigious area designated as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2021. There are over 40 monuments and over 40 buildings on the site. It’s easily one of the most picturesque and historic areas of the city.

The route begins at the Prado Museum, one of the best museums on the planet. Here you’ll find works from El Greco, Velázquez, and Goya, as well as many other masters (such as Rubens, Botticelli, and Caravaggio to name a few). If you only visit one museum in Madrid, this is the one. It’s incredible and worth taking the time to explore. It’s one of the biggest museums in the world, too. Make sure you spend a few hours here at a minimum.

Industry observers note that just a 10-minute walk along the Paseo del Prado, the journey continues at the Thyssen-Bornemisza Museum, a private collection spanning from the Renaissance to Pop Art, and culminates at the Reina Sofía Museum. The Reina Sofía National Art Center offers a fantastic collection of modern art. Works by masters like Picasso, Miró, Kandinsky, Dalí, and Bacon can all be found here. The centerpiece is Picasso’s famous Guernica, a 1937 oil painting considered the most moving anti-war painting in the world. While I don’t love modern art, even I enjoyed this museum.

It has been revealed that after museum hopping, it’s time to dive into Madrid’s culinary scene. Try Taberna La Fragua de Vulcano for a rustic atmosphere perfect for sampling cocido madrileño. If you are near the Reina Sofía Museum, don’t miss the vibrant garden terrace at Arzábal, renowned for having some of the best croquetas in the city. Finally, for a unique setting, Bodega de los Secretos lets you dine in restored 17th-century wine caves, making it the most atmospheric choice near the Prado Museum.

According to recent reports, after a late lunch, spend some time exploring Madrid’s unique ‘House Museums. These are former private palaces that preserve the intimate atmosphere of their original owners. The crown jewel of this collection is the Sorolla Museum, the sun-drenched former residence of ‘the painter of light.’ Following a major architectural renovation, this underrated museum is set to reopen its doors in 2026, offering a refreshed look at its stunning gardens and Mediterranean canvases.

Or if you want something else, there is also the nearby Museum of Romanticism, where you can enjoy a coffee in its secret garden, or visit the Lázaro Galdiano Museum to marvel at a private collection of Goya, Murillo, Velázquez, El Greco, or Bosch housed in a magnificent neo-Renaissance mansion.

In the evening, enjoy some food and relaxation.

Sources indicate that the second day delves into the medieval and Renaissance layout of the city, famously known as Habsburg Madrid (Madrid de los Austrias). The central hub is Puerta del Sol, where a photo at Kilometer Zero and the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue are mandatory for a traveler’s geographic check-in. Kilometer Zero is the official starting point of all the highways and railways in the country, making this effectively the center of the entire country. There’s a small plaque you can snap a photo of.

According to recent reports, nearby is the Bear and the Strawberry Tree statue (El Oso y el Madroño). The statue shows a bear reaching up to eat fruit from a madroño tree, symbols which come from Madrid’s coat of arms (the bear represents the city and the tree represents the land and nature surrounding it that has helped make it prosper).

Sources indicate that from here, walk toward the iconic Plaza Mayor, highlighting its porticoed architecture and the Casa de la Panadería. Plaza Mayor once hosted bullfights, markets, symphonies, tournaments, and even executions. Now it’s ringed with tourist shops, cafés, and restaurants. It’s a good place from which to indulge in some people-watching, offers some good (though overpriced) bars, and occasionally has concerts and events.

For a true “Local Life” experience, stop for a calamari sandwich in the nearby alleys. Your taste buds will thank you.

After a relaxing lunch and some people watching, head to the Royal Palace of Madrid. The largest palace in Western Europe, the Baroque-style palace was built in the 18th century and is home to over 3,400 lavishly decorated rooms. It was originally built on a former 9th-century Muslim fort and today functions much like an art museum with numerous works, including pieces by Caravaggio, Juan de Flandes, and Francisco Goya. Though it’s the official residence of the royal family, they don’t actually live here anymore, and the palace is only used for official state functions. You can walk through the palace (both self-guided and guided tours are available), starting at the grand stairway, and wander through lavishly decorated staterooms. There’s also the Royal Armory, which houses a collection of medieval weapons and armor.

According to recent reports, to end the day, head to the Almudena Cathedral. Unlike many of the famous medieval churches in Europe, this one was constructed in the late 19th century. It was finally completed in 1993 and was consecrated by Pope John Paul II. While the exterior has a Neo-Classical design (to match the nearby palace), the cathedral also has a Neo-Romanesque crypt with over 400 columns that you can explore. Be sure to head up to the dome for stunning views out over the city.

Sources indicate that madrid is a paradise for foodies. It’s one of the reasons I keep coming back. While there are plenty of food tours to take in Madrid, I suggest heading off on your own to explore. Begin at the city’s iconic gastronomic markets. The glass-walled Mercado de San Miguel is a must for gourmet tapas near Plaza Mayor. It’s popular with the after-work crowd and is a place I usually visit a few times on my trips. Additionally, local favorites like Mercado de San Antón in Chueca and Mercado de Vallehermoso offer a deeper dive into regional flavors. Just make sure to bring an appetite.

If you do want to take a food tour, consider doing a food tour. This post has more of my suggestions.

In a recent development, for dinner, head to Sobrino de Botín, officially recognized by the Guinness World Records as the world’s oldest restaurant. It was actually a favorite of Ernest Hemingway during his time in Madrid. For a more casual vibe, go ‘tapas crawling’ through the historic streets of La Latina or Barrio de las Letras.

According to recent reports, as the sun sets, head to the Gran Vía to experience Madrid’s world-class rooftop culture. Venues like The Roof at Picalagartos or RIU, 360º sky bar offer signature cocktails and dinner with breathtaking 360-degree views of the skyline.

For those who don’t eat meat, Madrid has actually evolved into one of Europe’s best veg hubs, boasting a vibrant vegetarian and vegan scene in neighborhoods like Malasaña, where plant-based versions of traditional Spanish dishes are now a staple of the city’s diverse culinary identity.

Madrid is the only European capital where nature, science, and royal history converge in a UNESCO World Heritage oasis known as the ‘Paisaje de la Luz‘ (Landscape of Light). But this prestigious area, encompassing the iconic El Retiro Park and the Paseo del Prado, is just the beginning of Spain’s monumental legacy. For more UNESCO wonders, take a day trip out of the city.

One popular destination worth visiting is the Monastery of San Lorenzo de El Escorial, a sprawling imperial masterpiece recognized by UNESCO for its historical significance. El Escorial is located just one hour from the city by car and was commissioned by Philip II in the 16th century. It’s a massive palatial complex that includes a monastery, library, palace, basilica, and tomb for Spanish monarchs. Yet as massive as it is, it feels more austere than other palatial complexes, likely owing to its granite walls and symmetrical layout.

Another option for a day trip is the Royal Palace and Gardens of Aranjuez, a World Heritage Cultural Landscape that rivals the beauty of Versailles. Located just one hour south of the city, this was originally a hunting lodge, also commissioned in the 16th century by Philip II. It’s a blend of Renaissance and Baroque styles, with lavish rooms filled with tapestries, porcelain, and ornate decorations. There is lots of greenery and gardens here, which is partly why the royal family used this as their spring residence.

According to recent reports, lastly, there’s the historic university city of Alcalá de Henares, the birthplace of Spanish novelist, poet, and playwright Cervantes (he wrote Don Quixote). Just 45 minutes away by car, it also holds its own UNESCO World Heritage status, offering a perfectly preserved look into the Spanish Golden Age (1492–1659).

In a recent development, on your last day, it’s time to get further off the beaten path. Step back into the Golden Age at the Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales and the nearby Royal Monastery of La Encarnación, two hidden palaces that house breathtaking royal art collections behind their cloistered walls.

The Monastery of Las Descalzas Reales is a convent founded in 1559 by Joanna of Austria (sister of Philip II). The name “Descalzas Reales” (which means “Royal Barefoot Ladies”) refers to the Order of Saint Clare nuns who lived here in relative austerity. What makes this monastery unique is that many aristocratic women took refuge here, often bringing their artworks and other valuables. Over the years, this turned the convent into a veritable treasure trove of art.

Recent findings suggest that the Royal Monastery of La Encarnación was founded in 1611 by the wife of Philip III, Margaret of Austria. It was a royal convent, meaning it had the direct support of the monarchy. While the exterior has an austere Baroque style, the interior is quite lavish, with ornate chapels, colorful frescoes, and lots of religious sculptures and paintings. It’s also home to several notable relics, including a vial said to contain the blood of Saint Januarius. While tours are available, it’s still an active convent so parts are not open to the public (which, honestly, makes it all the more interesting to see).

Industry observers note that to end your day with a local touch, head to the vast Casa de Campo park. This is the largest public park in the city, created in 1931. It covers a whopping 17 square kilometers (6.5 square miles) and includes an artificial lake, lots of paths, a zoo, and even an amusement park. Here, you can enjoy a scenic lunch or dinner at one of the lakeside terraces, offering an unrivaled view of the Royal Palace and Almudena Cathedral across the skyline. It’s the perfect place to end your trip.

It has been revealed that while Barcelona tends to get more attention, I think Madrid is one of the best cities in Europe. It boasts a mouthwatering culinary scene, a raucous nightlife, and tons of things to see and do — no matter your interest or budget. I’ve been visiting the city for almost two decades and never get tired of the tapas, architecture, and history. The city just packs so much in and there really is something for everyone here. By following the itinerary above, you’ll see all the main sights while also getting off the beaten path in Spain’s historic capital.

#54069. Some Democrats doubt Trump is serious about cutting deals in newly introduced Congress

Some Democrats doubt Trump is serious about cutting deals in newly introduced Congress

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that president Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct.
  • President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.
  • On the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the upcoming Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that president Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 13 before leaving for a campaign rally in Alaska. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

On the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the upcoming Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill. But on the other, he promoted his hard-line aide Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, raising doubts about any cooling of the political environment.

At every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov. 3, Trump railed against “Dumbocrats” and their “bad” policies. He mocked their candidates as too extreme, too corrupt and too beholden to the most progressive wing of their party. He even warned that, if voters handed them control of the House and Senate, it would set off “a 1929-style economic depression.”.

Voters ignored him. They handed House Democrats over 250 seats at least come January, and the party will have at least 54 seats in the Senate.

It has been revealed that trump was asked during a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday afternoon at the White House if he could resist insulting Democratic lawmakers for six months if that’s how long it took to reach a deal on major legislation. “Very easily,” he responded.

But several Democrats are so sure about getting to a “Kumbaya” moment with Trump during his final two years.

According to recent reports, virginia Sen. Tim Kaine said it was hard to take the president at his word because he is “so unpredictable.”.

“But I'm certainly telling my colleagues we should try to put as many bills as we can on his desk that do good things for the American public, and then see how he behaves,” he stated Tuesday.

"We're gonna put bills in front of the president on affordability starting Day One,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight and Government Reform chair, said Tuesday. “We'll have to see if he's serious, but I don't trust Donald Trump for a second.”.

The White House on Monday sent Garcia a letter, obtained by CQ Roll Call, warning House Democrats that their anticipated spate of probes "may cross the line into blatant criminality.".

Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat who is in line to chair the Rules Committee in the new Congress, stated on the floor Tuesday that he does not see a GOP that is ready to heed the election's lessons and come to the bargaining table.

“Instead of taking the hint or listening to the overwhelming majority of Americans who told them to change course, Republicans are doubling down on the same tactics and messaging they've been jamming down our throats these last two years, and it's a perfect example of why they lost in the first place,” he said. “They do not listen.

It has been revealed that “Then to double down even further, the failed lame-duck president appointed Stephen Miller, the architect of all the cruel policies that most people hate, as his newly introduced White House chief of staff,” McGovern added, referring to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. “What planet are these people living on?”.

Kaine said congressional Democrats might not notice that much of a change from the White House with Miller moving into the chief’s suite near the Oval Office.

Sources indicate that “Stephen Miller was calling a lot of the shots, even if he wasn't chief of staff,” the Virginia Democrat remarked. “So I view that as a kind of a change of the face, but not of the character of the administration.”.

House Republicans’ Tuesday vote to make hard-line conservative Jim Jordan of Ohio their next leader is another red flag for Democrats.

“White House Chief of staff Stephen Miller and House Minority Leader Jim Jordan,” Brendan Duke, a former senior Democratic Senate aide now with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, wrote on X. “Where is the pivot to the center after a historic election loss?”.

Getting to the center is what retiring Nebraska Rep. Don Bacon says his fellow Republicans and Trump should be doing after the election massacre.

"I do wish we could get to the point where we could solve big problems, instead of just beating the other side,” mentioned Bacon, who has floated a 2028 presidential bid. “We can’t do this Republican-only or Democrat-only. And I would say this to the president, too: We’ve got to start working across the aisle to solve these problems.”.

Sources indicate that despite his postelection talk of working with Democrats, Trump has sought to blame them for an up-and-down U.S. stock market.

Industry observers note that “Right after the election it went down $3 trillion,” he mentioned Monday during an unplanned White House press briefing. “That was because of the result of the election, because the stock market does not want to see Democrats. And your 401(k)s have gone way down because of the ridiculous result.”.

He's also returned this week to questioning the midterm results: “It's not even a result. It's almost hard to believe. Now, I wasn't on the ballot.”.

Industry observers note that members of House Republicans’ latest leadership team on Tuesday sounded dug in and ready for a partisan brawl over Democrats’ promised investigations into the president, many of his top aides and Trump family members. Jordan's election as GOP leader highlights that “we are ready to dig in for the fight,” outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Tuesday.

Michigan Rep. Lisa McClain, who was reelected House GOP conference chair, pointed to Garcia's two-word statement on Election Day: "Lawyer up.".

“Tell me how ‘lawyering up’ helps anybody with affordability?" she said. “They're going to be focused on going after President Trump. We are going to be focused on improving the quality of life for every American.”.

To that end, retiring Maryland Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, a former No. 2 House Democrat, remarked Republicans should heed one substantial takeaway from the election: “Trump lost.”.

  • The new Kindle is officially Amazon's most pocket-sized e-reader yet, featuring a redesigned flush-front display that eliminates the raised border around the screen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Amazon just gave its Kindle lineup a major makeover, and the smallest model might be the most exciting. Earlier this month, the manufacturer introduced a redesigned 6-inch Kindle that's more compact than any e-reader users have seen before. It’s got a sleek new look, faster performance, and four gorgeous colors that make the popular device feel like a cute accessory in its own right. After spending some time with the new Alpine Sky version, I can confidently say that its tiny size is one of my favorite things about it.

The new Kindle is officially Amazon's most pocket-sized e-reader yet, featuring a redesigned flush-front display that eliminates the raised border around the screen. The 6-inch, 300-ppi glare-free display is still black and white, but the device itself now has color that stretches seamlessly from front to back. Amazon also claims the new Kindle opens books 30 percent faster than its predecessor and offers up to six weeks of battery life on a single charge, which has been ideal for me, someone who forgets to charge any of his devices.

One of the biggest updates is the introduction of two different versions of the 6-inch Kindle. The standard model starts at $149.99 and comes in Ube (a pretty purple shade) and classic Graphite, with 16 GB of storage. For $189.99, you can upgrade to the upcoming Kindle Aluminum, which comes in Alpine Sky and Seaglass Green, with a premium matte aluminum back, 32GB of storage, and no lock-screen ads.

I have the Alpine Sky version, which has a beautiful, soft blue finish that always gets compliments from friends. But beyond the new colors and materials, I've appreciated most how easy this little thing is to bring everywhere. I live in New York City, so I'm constantly taking the subway, and carrying a physical book around isn't always convenient. It’s not impossible, but it can be a nuisance when I'm reading something particularly thick. The Kindle is smaller than most of the books I own, takes up little room in my bag, and feels comfortable to hold for longer reading sessions without making my hand ache.

It has been revealed that I also love that I can throw it into pretty much any bag I'm carrying, whether it's a small everyday bag or something much larger. And, admittedly, there's something funny about watching other commuters on the subway notice it. I swear I can see people clocking the tiny blue Kindle and thinking how cute it is (but that could just be my main-character energy). The text is still plenty readable despite its smaller display, and sometimes I feel like the person sitting next to me is following along with whatever chapter I'm on.

Sources indicate that of course, the smaller Kindle doesn't have every feature you'll find on Amazon's pricier models. It lacks waterproofing and adjustable warm lighting like the Kindle Paperwhite, so readers who prioritize those features may prefer the larger option. But if you want a convenient, portable way to read, there's plenty to appreciate here.

The fresh 6-inch Kindle and Kindle Aluminum are available to shop now, with prices starting at $149.99. Whether you're new to e-reading or just want something smaller for your commute, Amazon's latest release makes a pretty convincing case for carrying an entire library in your bag.

Breaking: Deadline looms for post-9/11 FirstNet reauthorization

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug.
  • Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.
  • A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug. 11, 2023 in Lahaina, Hawaii. The performance of the FirstNet network during the Maui fires has partially led to calls for a revamp of its structure. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images).

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any new bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

According to recent reports, the House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances.

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., mentioned in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

“Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

It has been revealed that “Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”.

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At issue in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

The Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura said his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change.

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

Jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He remarked that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”.

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, remarked that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He noted the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”.

Ors remarked he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely new bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A new Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

Congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco said he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

Industry observers note that the House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a latest version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • According to recent reports, when it comes to backcountry safety, there’s no messing around.
  • Used for decades, walkie-talkies are a lesser-talked-about gadget for hikers, campers, paddlers, bikers, skiers, and more heading into the wilderness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, when it comes to backcountry safety, there’s no messing around. Serious adventure seekers know it’s best to prepare for their outdoor escapades—whether they’re heading deep into the wilderness or staying close to home. If not, you risk injury or worse. From a reliable fixed-blade knife to a solid pair of binoculars for scouting the trail ahead, there’s a whole slew of gear to keep you safe outdoors.

Used for decades, walkie-talkies are a lesser-talked-about gadget for hikers, campers, paddlers, bikers, skiers, and more heading into the wilderness. Yet this humble piece of equipment plays an important role in helping you communicate with colleagues, friends, and family when you’re on the go. They’re also a smart backup in an emergency and a way to monitor the weather in untamed landscapes and far-off places.

Recent findings suggest that today’s walkie-talkies haven’t changed all too much in look and feel from their early days. But they’re nothing like the cheap, toy versions we used as kids when exploring backyard “wilderness.” Modern features like NOAA weather alerts, VOX (hands-free operation), and app-connected features provide safeguards and peace of mind—especially in faraway places.

Our guide below covers what to keep in mind and how to choose a walkie-talkie for work, play, and emergencies—and offers a closer look at standout models worth your money.

Recent findings suggest that our evaluation process combined rigorous field testing across a wide variety of walkie-talkies in different environments with extensive research from trusted online sources. Meehan’s in-field testing for his best two-way radio picks ranged from trekking deep into the backcountry on hut trips to communicating seamlessly while mountain biking to traveling around a city.

Recognizing that walkie-talkies serve a wide audience, we also considered other scenarios where dependable communication is essential—on construction sites, inside expansive venues like convention centers, and across large retail operations.

With this breadth of uses in mind, we reviewed models spanning a range of functions and price points, carefully weighing usability, durability, range, features, and cost. For radios we couldn’t test directly, we reviewed trusted sources and compared specs. We also factored in real-world customer feedback, ensuring our final selections reflect not only expert insights but also everyday user experiences.

Recent findings suggest that these Midland radios have proven reliable in the city and the mountains. The two-pack is a great value and includes advanced features like hands-free VOX and NOAA weather channel monitoring.

Recent findings suggest that it's one of the most versatile walkie-talkies in terms of power options. As part of a two-pack, you get a charging cradle for each, but you can also charge the device with a micro-USB cable and, if you’re in the field for multiple days and run out of power, you can switch the battery pack out for a new one or use three AA batteries to power it—though it is hard to get the cover off.

Industry observers note that the radios are compatible with multiple accessories, like a hand-held mic-speaker or an earpiece-mic combo. The latter makes hands-free use even easier, like in a restaurant or store setting.

In a recent development, the walkies boast 36 channels, some preconfigured for privacy. With privacy codes, it has 121 channels in total. The speaker and mic aren't as crisp as some other models, and the range isn’t as great as others.

But in the end, this relatively affordable set of walkies has an ideal feature set for most people.

It shouldn’t surprise that a organization known for its smartphones, like the Razr+, would add smartphone-like features to its top-line walkie-talkies. That’s exactly what Motorola did with its 800-series Talkabout line.

It uses the Talkabout app for iOS and Android devices to enable features other walkie-talkies can’t, like letting you use the 800 series as a sort of smartphone modem when there’s no cell service.

Recent findings suggest that the app also lets you send texts or share your location with others using an 800-series radio and the app. This feature is unavailable on most walkie-talkies, since they’re just two-way radios. It also supports smart pairing and connects to Bluetooth devices, like headphones or earbuds.

Beyond that, the 800 series Talkabout offers the features you’d expect in a good-quality walkie-talkie with access to the 22 FRS channels and 121 privacy codes. This T803 radio has advantages over the T800 (for example, a better weatherproof rating) and the T802, which doesn’t come with a rechargeable battery.

Most walkie-talkies on the market are waterproof, or at the very least water-resistant, since they’re meant for outdoor use. But you’ll find it harder to find a two-way radio that can actually float. That’s where Cobra's floating walkie-talkies stand out.

Recent findings suggest that built to IPX7 waterproof standards, this radio can survive full immersion underwater and is designed to float—ideal for situations like water sports, boating, paddling, skiing, and backcountry adventures. This walkie-talkie can handle dunkings and wet environments where communication is critical, and its orange rubber exterior makes it easy to spot in choppy surf or on snow-covered slopes.

Best for whitewater kayakers, stand-up paddle boarders, or even families enjoying a long weekend on the boat, it's a solid pick when you want to stay connected without worrying about waterlogging. You won’t have to worry about sinking or failing when wet. This durability is also ideal for backcountry skiers or climbers who deal with wet conditions daily.

Extra features like voice-activated transmission (aka hands-free talking) and the ability to replay missed radio calls also pack a punch. With its 37-mile range, NOAA weather alerts, and an impressive 2662 channel combinations, this Cobra radio is more than just waterproof—it’s an essential tool for adventurers heading into rugged, remote environments.

In the end, it’s hard to deny the Rocky Talkie Mountain Radio's capabilities compared to others made for outdoor adventure. It could easily have been our top pick, but since not everyone goes on multi-day backcountry trips, the Mountain Radio is likely overkill for most.

Recent findings suggest that founded in 2019, RockyTalkie is a newcomer to the scene, but it has nailed it with this 2-watt FRS radio with great range. Even in forested, mountainous areas, we could still easily communicate over miles. It also had one of the longest-lasting batteries, even in freezing weather.

Sources indicate that the Mountain Radio sports a really simple interface with just five buttons, and it’s easy to lock onto a channel. The radio also has a great speaker and microphone for transmitting and receiving calls and a bright green LED display that disappears when the radio isn’t actively transmitting or receiving.

We also appreciate the radio's rugged, rubberized outer shell and its two removable attachment points. The device uses carabiners rather than belt clips like most other two-way radios. That makes it easy to attach to just about anything—a harness, a belt loop, a backpack strap, a PFD, and more. The secondary attachment point uses smaller carabiners and a coiled leash, making it even harder to drop or lose.

The only thing we found lacking in the radio is that it can’t scan and play NOAA weather alerts, which would be very helpful in a backcountry setting with no access to cell service.

Industry observers note that the Rocky Talkie 5-Watt Radio showcases backcountry endurance at its finest. It’s beefed-up, replaceable battery lasts up to six full days on a single charge. That’s nearly a week of reliable communication without scrambling for a power bank or solar panel to plug into while off-grid—making it one of the longest-lasting walkie-talkies in its class.

Recent findings suggest that this two-way radio also shines for its durability, with an IP67 waterproof and dustproof rating. It also includes NOAA weather alerts, dual-frequency monitoring, and up to 5 watts of transmitting power for extended range. An important note: you need a GMRS license to operate this radio legally in the field.

While its design is compact, it’s heavier than many other walkie-talkies we tested. That said, for the peace of mind that comes with extended battery life and a durable design that tops our list for its rugged, waterproof build, you can’t go wrong with this radio.

Bottom line: the Rocky Talkie 5-Watt is our go-to choice for lasting power and rugged dependability.

Recent findings suggest that while it’s technically not a walkie-talkie, the Garmin InReach Mini 2 deserves a spot in any serious communication roundup. For backcountry adventures where two-way communication is less frequent or a walkie-talkie just won’t cut it, this pocket-sized satellite device becomes a lifeline—especially when cell service and radio coverage fail.

The InReach Mini 2 uses the Iridium satellite network to deliver global coverage wherever you roam. You can send two-way text messages, share GPS location, and trigger SOS alerts from literally anywhere in the world. This piece of tech is best described as a satellite phone stripped down to the essentials: sending and receiving messages without overcomplicating communications.

It weighs a mere 3.5 ounces, and its compact design lets you clip the sat-phone to your pack or strap, or slide it into your pocket. You can also sync the InReach Mini 2 with Garmin’s Earthmate app for easier texting if you have your phone with you on your adventures.

Another big selling point of this piece of gear over walkie-talkies is its 14-day lifespan—long enough for extended off-grid trips. Unlike FRS or GMRS walkie-talkies, which are limited by terrain and line-of-sight requirements, this communication device promises to keep you in touch with family and friends wherever your adventures take you. Even more importantly, it keeps you connected in an emergency.

It has been revealed that while a walkie-talkie is a simple, handheld, portable two-way radio, not all are the same. Some are designed for indoor use, while others are meant for outdoor use. Some suit adventurers and sportspeople, while others offer features best suited to first responders. And, of course, some are designed for kids. When selecting the right two-way radios for your needs, there are plenty of factors to consider.

Industry observers note that the basics are battery life, transmitting power or range, durability, weather/waterproofness, and remote capabilities. More advanced features include weather channels, VOX (voice-operated exchange, which is hands-free voice-activated transmission), access to NOAA weather channels, the ability to monitor multiple channels, privacy codes, headset ports, repeater channels, and NFC and Bluetooth connections.

Most walkie-talkies are Family Radio Service (FRS) units with 2 watts or less of broadcasting power. These need no license. Devices that have more than 2 watts of broadcasting power, up to 50 watts, are called General Mobile Radio Service (GMRS) units.

GMRS devices require an FCC license. However, as the folks at Rocky Talkie explain on their site, it’s pretty easy to get one online in the U.S. It costs $35 and is good for 10 years, covering everyone in your immediate family. The higher the wattage, the more transmitting power and range the walkie-talkie has, which generally means it uses more power and has a larger antenna. You can see that difference pretty clearly between the Rocky Talkie 5-Watt Radio and the brand’s smaller 2-watt Mountain Radio.

Both types of units can broadcast on a range of channels, and each channel has wattage restrictions. Channels 1 through 7 can broadcast at up to 5 watts. Channels 8 through 14 can only broadcast at up to 0.5 watts. Channels 15 through 22 can broadcast at up to 50 watts, making them ideal for communications up to 30 miles apart in good conditions.

Recent findings suggest that some walkie-talkies can broadcast on other channels, but it's not recommended, as emergency and first responders may use them, and it’s illegal to broadcast on them. On the other hand, some Midland radios list “additional channels.” But in that case, they’re existing channels with pre-set privacy codes.

It has been revealed that speaking of, when using walkie talkies with a group of people it’s always notable to check that everyone is on the same channel, and if using a private channel to reduce interference from others, that everyone is on the same privacy code. We’d also recommend locking the devices to that channel—unless you need to be on multiple channels or scanning channels.

Not all two-way radios are designed with the same level of user-friendliness and a simple interface. The interface plays a major role in how easy the device is to use, especially when in the field with limited bandwidth for fidgeting with buttons and screen controls. Some radios keep things simple with large knobs and backlit buttons that let you seamlessly switch channels or adjust volume with a quick twist or tap—even while wearing gloves. Others rely on small digital menus that can be challenging to navigate, especially while on the go.

In a recent development, and some advanced walkie-talkies even require setup, such as programming frequencies through a computer and cables. While this may give more control, it can intimidate newer two-way radio owners.

In a recent development, when comparing radios, pay attention to details like clearly marked buttons, backlit displays for night use, and easy setup processes. Features like one-touch scanning or memory recall can be great options when you need quick, efficient communication. Ultimately, the best radio delivers reliable performance without sacrificing user experience—especially when it matters most in the field.

It has been revealed that most two-way radios use replaceable batteries, usually AA or AAA, rechargeable batteries, or sometimes can use either. Units with rechargeable batteries are often more expensive, but usually have good longevity for trail and backcountry use. Some units recharge in a cradle but ideally also have a port for charging via a DC or USB cable, allowing you to power up from a backup battery as needed. We’ve left units on overnight before and still had power in the morning, and some will go into a low-power mode when left on. The battery will last longer if you use the walkie less or use a lower wattage mode, but that will also reduce its transmitting and receiving range.

Industry observers note that obviously, you want your devices to last a long time, and walkie-talkies should endure for years and withstand knocks and drops. That's why most don’t have touchscreens or even glass screens. Most should be able to withstand minor spills or rain, but if you know you’ll be using them primarily in the water, like on a fishing boat or white-water rafting and kayaking, you’ll want a walkie-talkie that’s waterproof and carries an IP67 rating or higher. If you’re using walkies in the backcountry or on a job site, you’ll want two-way radios that are ruggedized—like the DeWalt 2-Watt Heavy-Duty Walkie-Talkie or Rocky Talkies—and can withstand drops better than some others.

Sources indicate that walkie-talkies offer a few options for remote operation. Some will allow VOX or hands-free operation and are activated by your voice. Others have wired microphones and speakers that are handheld or worn on a lapel or shoulder strap. Others have an earpiece and microphone. Some modern walkie-talkies can actually pair with Bluetooth earpieces, also allowing for hands-free communication. This is great when wearing a motorcycle helmet or when a wire could get in the way of whatever you’re doing.

Some models have additional channel monitoring or communication capabilities, like operating on two frequencies at the same time. These are handy features, but using them will drain the battery faster while they’re on.

Walkie-talkies designed for outdoor use, for example, can monitor NOAA weather channels, giving you some insight into the weather and the conditions you may face while camping, driving off-road, hiking, or hunting that you otherwise wouldn’t be able to access.

In a recent development, still others can communicate and monitor two channels at the same time. That could allow you to communicate with multiple teams at once. For instance, in a rescue situation, you could communicate with your friends on one channel and the local sheriff’s office or the search-and-rescue team on another without switching channels every time.

While all walkie-talkie channels are open to all consumers, some are generally used by certain groups and/or in certain areas. You can talk with local organizations to find out which channels they use and broadcast on.

To help people connect with like minds, some are encouraging what they call community channels. These help people in a local backcountry area communicate with each other. Rocky Talkie lists some active community channels for local areas. While these channels help in some situations, you also don’t want to communicate constantly on channels monitored by SAR or local sheriff’s offices, because you could interrupt emergency operations.

Recent findings suggest that walkie-talkies come in a wide range of prices, and more expensive models often offer more benefits and features. So, while you can get a serviceable pair for about $30-$35, they won’t have much range or additional features. For a top-tier single walkie-talkie with multi-channel monitoring, high wattage and range, and water- and shock-proofing, you can expect to pay over $150 per unit.

Industry observers note that range is one of the biggest selling points for walkie-talkies, but it’s also one of the most misunderstood. Sure, the box may say “up to 35 miles of range.” That’s only if conditions are near-perfect—think one person on a mountain peak and another down in a valley, with nothing but clear air between them. In reality, terrain, obstructions, severe weather (like a snowstorm), and more can drastically cut that range. Dense forest, rocky canyons, massive hills, and buildings can shrink that range even more.

According to recent reports, most consumer FRS models perform best up to five miles, depending on the terrain. For most outdoor adventures, a reliable one-to-five-mile range is typical and usually enough to keep track of groups across rivers, campsites, or trails. GMRS radios, which we mentioned require a license, can stretch much further than five miles, especially when paired with repeaters.

Our recommendation: Shop for a walkie-talkie model and range based on realistic expectations for your use case, not the maximum range advertised in the brand’s marketing.

Industry observers note that it depends! How often and for how long do you proposal to use your radio? Are you looking for a basic radio or one built to perform off-grid? Battery life depends most on design and how often you use it. Most walkie-talkies advertise a battery lifespan of eight to 20 hours of runtime, but those numbers assume moderate to infrequent use. Continuous transmission drains the battery much faster than standby mode.

Sources indicate that for shorter day hikes and quick outings, you won’t have to worry much about your radio lasting more than a single charge. On longer excursions, opt for a walkie-talkie that can be charged via USB-C with an external battery pack, or that uses AA or AAA batteries. Simply put: Don’t trust what the packaging claims. Instead, consider how long you plan to use the two-way radio and whether you’ll have a chance to recharge partway through a long adventure.

It has been revealed that many modern two-way radios offer more than basic push-to-talk functionality. NOAA weather alerts are especially helpful for backcountry safety, providing real-time updates on weather patterns and severe storms heading your way.

According to recent reports, another feature to look for is VOX—voice-activated transmission—which enables hands-free use. Paddlers, bikers, and skiers are prime candidates for VOX-equipped walkie-talkies when devices aren’t always easy to grab while in motion.

Other bonus features to look for include the ability to scan multiple channels, privacy codes to reduce interference from strangers, and built-in flashlights and SOS alarm signaling in emergencies.

For simple day-hiking trail use or communicating with your family across the campground, simple models will work just fine. But on bigger adventures like backpacking into the wilderness and remote paddling, investing in a two-way radio with all the bells and whistles gives you peace of mind and the right tools when conditions are worse than expected.
