💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that it’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded.
  • And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.
  • As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

Recent findings suggest that in the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

But now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Sources indicate that beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

In a recent development, the trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

It has been revealed that as an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

The 40 Best Resorts in Mexico: 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards

📅 13 Jan 2015 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1880 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Trends come and go, but here at Condé Nast Traveler, one thing never changes: your insatiable appetite for seeing the world.
  • View all of the Readers’ Choice Awards winners for 2026 here.
  • The most distinctive part of Hilton’s luxury debut on Mexico’s Riviera Maya is its chameleon-like approach to hospitality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Trends come and go, but here at Condé Nast Traveler, one thing never changes: your insatiable appetite for seeing the world. This year, our readers cast an almighty 798,867 votes in our 39th Readers’ Choice Awards to tell us about the planet’s best travel experiences: You fell hard for palace hotels in Morocco, cruised down the Amazon, and got swept up in Latest York City’s exhilarating energy. Now, read on to find out where your favorites fall among the winners—and get inspired for where to go next, whether it's to a top-rated hotel or resort, or a TK centered around a worthy cruise, spa, or island. These are the best resorts in the world as voted by you, our readers.

View all of the Readers’ Choice Awards winners for 2026 here.

The most distinctive part of Hilton’s luxury debut on Mexico’s Riviera Maya is its chameleon-like approach to hospitality. Yes, with its 349 rooms, acres of pools, 11 restaurants, and kids’ and teens’ clubs, the Conrad is the type of resort whose (large bronze) gates a traveler would be content to pass through only twice: right before check-in and right after checkout. Spiritually, though, it aligns more closely with the smaller-scale properties 30 minutes north in Tulum that seek to connect guests with the surrounding destination. Honoring the Mayan cultures that have occupied this stretch of Caribbean coast for centuries, a traditional sacbe, or “white road”—the name of the ancient roadways Mayans created to travel by moonlight—cuts through the jungled grounds. In the lobby, a soaring art installation takes a cue from Mayan macramé. And at the cenote-inspired spa, a traditional four-hands massage is second only to a jalapeño margarita in the open-air bar as a way to immediately shed any lingering real-life stress remaining after a dip in the sea.

Beaches with sand as soft as silk and water as pure as a turquoise gem sound like a dream, and the balmy surroundings of the Hyatt Zilara Riviera Maya make that vision a reality. An adult-only resort just a 30-minute drive away from Cancun International Airport (CUN), this Hyatt outpost makes booking in some much-needed R&R more convenient than ever. The beach is truly at your fingertips at this reader-favorite hideaway with swim-up suites, bars right on the shore, and the Zen Spa which perches right above it all. You may be parked at this bolthole in the Caribbean, but when it comes to your dining options, the world comes to you. The property houses seven bars and restaurants that cater to every palette, whether you're looking for coastal Italian one night or sushi the next.

Along a palm-studded stretch of coast in the Yucatán Peninsula is the recently opened SLS Playa Mujeres, a 498-room resort offering an array of suites, some with a private balcony, terrace, or a garden with a swim-out pool. The opening of SLS Playa Mujeres also marks the debut of SLS Elite, a selection of rooms offering benefits, including private lounge access, preferred dining reservations, and entry to an exclusive beach. Available to all guests on an all-inclusive basis are 18 restaurant and bar concepts, including Mediterranean-inspired dining at Fi’lia and Cleo, fresh catch at Caracol, and classic steakhouse fare at Union. At the heart of the resort is the 20,000-square-foot Ciel Spa, a wellness destination with thermal baths and an outdoor tranquility pool.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

It has been revealed that here, the first cocktail arrives before you do, served aboard the open-bar catamaran that carries you from Cancún to this adult-only retreat on Isla Mujeres. Joining Hyatt’s Unbound Collection in November 2026, Impression lives up to its name, with terraces cascading toward a sheltered beach and rooftop infinity pools that give you every reason to admire the water without venturing down to it. Each of the 125 suites comes with dedicated butler service and all-inclusive coverage, including gourmet à la carte dining. At Spezia, decadent Italian cooking offers a reason to dress for dinner, though your butler can arrange a quieter evening in, should you desire.

Opened in February 2022, this Costa Mujeres gem has become a winner for its stand-out dining (including a food truck and on-site Japanese restaurant) as well as a beachfront pool deck complete with a glass-sided infinity pool. The modern amenities and standout service make it clear this is a five-star property, and guests love the poolside sushi and steak as much as the vast beachfront and unending views.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Etéreo, Auberge Collection is only a 30-minute drive from the Cancún airport, but this slice of heaven on the Riviera Maya feels light-years away from the chaos. The resort is incredibly family-friendly, but not in a way that sacrifices any of its sophistication. It’s the type of place where you stay put and enjoy everything it has to offer, like luxurious spa treatments, unique culinary experiences, and pool and beachside lounging, unless you’re going on one of the excursions organized by the hotel, which range from water activities, like cenote exploration and sailing to a tour of the local archaeological zones. Every single one of the 75 rooms is ocean-facing, with floor to ceiling sliding glass doors framing the view, and leading to private terraces perched above the mangroves. Couples and families with young kids looking for an easy, peaceful escape would do well to book a stay at this intimate property.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Staying at the Viceroy Riviera Maya is a vacation in the truest sense of the word: Palapa villas with lots of wood and rattan (many with private pools and outdoor showers) are connected by meandering pathways that fan out to lush, fragrant gardens. And it’s all fronted by seven miles of glorious, white sand beaches. Just remember that you are in the jungle, so be sure to keep your eye out for wily spider monkeys.

Industry observers note that this palm-studded resort has been one of the most beloved destinations on the Riviera Maya since it opened in 1995. But a complete reimagining of the 72-room hotel has given it a renewed edge over its neighbors—without losing any of its soul. Arriving at Maroma involves driving through thick mangroves where spider monkeys swing from the trees (the property sits on 200 acres of jungle) before reaching its signature whitewashed architecture and thatched roofs. The design still leans heavily on the region’s Mayan vernacular—the curved stucco buildings are based on ancient geometric principles—and wider Mexican craftsmanship. In fact, almost every detail of the restoration, overseen by interior designer Tara Bernerd, prioritized Mexican makers and artisans (80 percent of the property’s furnishings and objects were made in the country), from the hand-painted Saltillo floor tiles and woven wall hangings to the cotton “manta” caftans left in rooms for guests to slip into. Rooms overlook the palm tree-lined pool, the Caribbean Sea, or both, and feature more of those beautiful tiles, along with whitewashed walls hung with regional textiles. Every detail is designed to keep guests rooted in the Yucatán Peninsula: Even the in-room bar, which is far from mini, is stocked with local spirits like pox, a Mayan liquor made of corn, sugarcane, and wheat, and Mayalen Guerrero mezcal in a beau­tiful bottle. Of the two restaurants on site, the pick is Casa Mayor from Mexican chef Daniel Camacho, which does mind-blowing tomato salads. (The chef also teaches a predictably delicious tortilla-making class.) While the property is spectacular, you shouldn’t miss the chance to explore the surroundings, which include a network of cenotes reached through underground caves. A swim in the pools, bats swooping overhead, is the stuff memories are made of. From $845. —Lale Arikoglu.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

Industry observers note that expect "a bit of Caribbean heaven" at this all-inclusive beach resort 20 minutes southwest of Puerto Morelos. Suites, some of which are swim-in/swim-out, are surrounded by 12 small pools and have views of "the most beautiful white sand beach." "Staff pamper you but respect your privacy." Sit under a palapa and enjoy seafood at Oceana; Himitsu has four teppanyaki grill tables. The 13,000-square-foot spa is "a wonderful refuge"—try the Papaya Passion, an exfoliation with papaya seeds and oils in a Vichy shower.

In a recent development, done up in a relaxing palette of Caribbean Sea blues, sandy beiges, and cumulus-cloud whites, the 371 rooms at this adults-only, all-inclusive resort are designed to set minds at ease at every turn. The hotel occupies an enviable strip of real estate on the Zona Hotelera waterfront, but guests won’t need to wander far to occupy time during their stays: The 11 bars, restaurants, and cafés include such standouts as Sea Corner for ceviches and tropical cocktails, while spa treatments draw on the aromas and ingredients of the region, including avocado, cocoa, and coffee.

For all the resorts that crowd Mexico’s east coast, the Waldorf stands out for its truly white-glove service and amenities that make it hard to leave the property. There are infinity pools aplenty, acres of pristine coastline, and that most glorious asset of all, the feeling of complete privacy in one of the country’s most bustling vacation spots. The decor, a soothing sea of creams and sand hues, spotlights Mexican artisans and highlights materials like tropical woods and local stone. The vibe here is palpably slow—no rushing from one activity to the next, just relaxing. And there are enough private cabanas to go around—you can forget about the dreaded visit to the pool at dawn to reserve a great spot. There are also dozens of lounge chairs facing the beach for when the ocean is your dip du jour. With comfortable yet polished rooms, an excellent spa, and a clutch of bars and restaurants serving excellent riffs on traditional dishes and drinks, this is Cancun like you’ve never seen it.

Industry observers note that at this all-inclusive, adults-only resort along the Riveria Maya, the food, spa treatments, and stellar views are the main attractions. Rooms and suites come with perks like private swim-up pools, outdoor spa tubs, and panoramic views, while the airy interiors feature wooden accents, hand-crafted furniture, and works made by local artists. Guests can opt for “local host” service: They will help arrange everything from a pillow menu request to an insider’s guide to the local food scene. Alternatively, take your pick from the five onsite restaurants—spanning Mediterranean, Mexican, Japanese, and European cuisines—including Cueva Siete, overseen by celebrity chef Xavier Perez Stone.

After its recent $50 million expansion, this is the star of the Mayakoba development in Playa del Carmen, with 34 private beachfront pool suites and a brand-fresh beach club with an infinity pool overlooking the ocean. Beneath wooden pergolas and linen umbrellas of the Sands Beach Club, city dwellers on a seaside escape bask in the balmy Yucatán air before the languid Caribbean waters of Riviera Maya. The development includes a waterway lined with mangroves perfect for kayaking excursions, over two miles of biking and walking trails, and a Greg Norman-designed, 18-hole golf course. The resort has its very own turtle field since, where four of the seven species worldwide come to nest on the beaches of the complex.

Check Availability at Booking.com.

#53982. Don’t Scan This Abroad: The QR Code Travel Scam Tourists Miss

📅 01 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1602 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theplanetd ↗ Open Full Page

Don’t Scan This Abroad: The QR Code Travel Scam Tourists Miss

📅 01 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1602 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theplanetd

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, QR codes are everywhere when we travel now, on restaurant tables, parking meters, hotel signs, airports, train stations, and transit machines.
  • According to recent reports, QR code travel scam happens when a fake QR code sends travellers to a fraudulent website.
  • Industry observers note that A scammer does not always need to hack a system or damage a payment machine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, QR codes are everywhere when we travel now, on restaurant tables, parking meters, hotel signs, airports, train stations, and transit machines. This travel scam known as Quishing or QR code phishing is becoming the fastest growing travel scam warning out there. Most QR codes are legitimate, but scammers are using fake QR code stickers and fake payment pages to catch travellers when they are tired, rushed, or distracted.

According to recent reports, QR code travel scam happens when a fake QR code sends travellers to a fraudulent website. The code may be placed over a real QR code on a parking meter, restaurant table, hotel notice, airport sign, or transit machine, or it may arrive by text or email pretending to be a fine, toll, ticket, or check-in request. The safest rule is simple: Pause. Check. Then pay.Read out post: 20 Common Travel Scams and How to Avoid Them.

Industry observers note that A scammer does not always need to hack a system or damage a payment machine. Sometimes they print a fake QR code sticker and place it directly over a legitimate code.

From a quick glance, the sign still looks official. The logo may look familiar. The instructions may seem normal. The page that opens may copy the colours, layout, and branding of the real organization.

Industry observers note that you think you are paying for parking, ordering food, checking into a hotel, or settling a toll. Instead, criminals may be collecting your credit card number, password, phone number, licence plate, email address, or other personal information.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that begin with a QR code and try to scare people into paying a fake unpaid balance.

The FTC has warned that scammers hide harmful links in QR codes to steal personal information, including by placing fake QR codes over real ones on parking meters.

Many restaurants now use QR codes for menus, ordering, or payment. Most are legitimate, but travellers should still be cautious. This is the easiest travel scam for QR code phishing as everyone uses it.

Industry observers note that A menu QR code should usually show a menu. Be careful if it asks for information it does not need, such as your passport number, banking details, hotel room number, or a password.

Before scanning a QR code on a restaurant table, look at the surface. Does it look printed into the menu or table sign, or does it look like a sticker placed on top? If it looks raised, crooked, bubbled, or mismatched, ask staff for a printed menu or the restaurant’s official website.

Parking is one of the easiest places for this scam to work because travellers are often rushed and confused.

According to recent reports, you may not know the local parking app. You may be dealing with another language. You may be worried about getting a ticket. That pressure makes a “scan to pay” sticker feel helpful.

Before paying through a parking QR code, inspect the sticker, read the URL preview, and check whether the payment page matches the city, parking authority, or official app named on the machine.

If anything feels off, do not use the QR code. Type the official website yourself, use the official parking app, pay at the machine, or ask local staff for help.

Airports and transit stations are full of QR codes: Wi-Fi, directions, tickets, luggage storage, forms, lounge access, and service information. Travel scams often happen when travelers are in a hurry. If you need wifi, a taxi, some food, QR codes are often the easiest way to catch you off guard.

According to recent reports, that does not mean every code is unsafe. It means you should slow down when a public QR code asks for payment, passwords, ID documents, or personal information.

The FBI warns that malicious QR codes can send people to fake sites, steal victim data, embed malware, or redirect payments. The FBI warns that criminals can tamper with QR codes to redirect payments, steal login and financial information, or send people to malicious websites.

The easiest way to avoid this scam is to build one habit before you scan a public QR code.

It has been revealed that do not scan just because a sign looks official. Public signs, parking meters, table cards, and posters can be tampered with.

Recent findings suggest that if the message says you must pay immediately, avoid a fine, settle a toll, confirm a booking, or prevent a penalty, slow down. Urgency is one of the biggest warning signs.

Before your phone opens anything, look at the QR code itself.

Sources indicate that sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally rolled out a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

The lame-duck session continues as lawmakers look ahead to Thanksgiving and the funding deadline that arrives in December. The primary legislative business this week is the Senate's bipartisan permitting overhaul, but a late-breaking aviation funding fight and the Senate Democratic leadership contest are also commanding attention.

Sources indicate that sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally debuted a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., and both men are accumulating supporters ahead of leadership votes that are at the moment scheduled for early December — though there's been an effort to move that up to this week.

Van Hollen has expressed disagreement with Schumer's participation in primaries.

​"I don't think it's the role of the Senate majority leader to get involved in open, contested Democratic primaries," Van Hollen mentioned Sunday on CNN.

​Van Hollen has also said he wants to use all available tools to stop funding for the Iran war immediately, with a government funding deadline in December. That's going to be one of several flash points for December's funding discussions, as President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans try to use what leverage they have before Democrats take the gavels in the House and the Senate in January.

A newly introduced issue is the state of federal air traffic control after Friday's nationwide ground stop, with the Trump administration now seeking $50 billion to upgrade systems.

"I need additional money to do the additional work to keep the airspace safe," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy mentioned on Fox News Sunday.

Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, a senior appropriator who is in line to become majority whip, has suggested reallocating funds from the additional money the Trump administration and congressional Republicans allocated to Immigration and Customs Enforcement to address the challenges at the Federal Aviation Administration.

Sources indicate that "There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA. We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars," Schatz posted on X.

"We can do all things, we don't have to do one versus the other," Duffy noted in the Fox News Sunday interview. "I don't think that is the answer. The answer is let's do everything that's going to keep Americans safe, whether it's with immigration or it's with air travel.".

Meanwhile on the Senate floor, the energy permitting overhaul bill faces a key test Monday evening​, with a vote scheduled to limit debate on a substitute amendment that represents the most recent version of the bill. Votes on a number of President Donald Trump's judicial nominations are also lined up this week.

On the other side of the Capitol, the House floor schedule i​ncludes several labor-related bills. ​One of the measures, introduced by Sen.-elect Kevin Hern, R-Okla.,​ would set standards for the way labor law applies to franchise operators.

Fresh member orientation is also continuing, and committees in both the House and Senate will be holding hearings throughout the week as the outgoing Republican committee chairs aim to get through priority items on their agenda before the end of the Congress.

That includes a Tuesday morning Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing for Hung Cao, the nominee to be Navy secretary, who is at the moment the acting secretary. The Senate Judiciary Committee will be busy as well, as Chairman Charles E. Grassley, R-Iowa, looks to tee up more of Trump's judicial nominations for floor consideration.

#53979. How to Blueprint a Trip to the World’s Largest Ski Resort, Les Trois Vallées

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2106 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cntraveler ↗ Open Full Page

How to Blueprint a Trip to the World’s Largest Ski Resort, Les Trois Vallées

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2106 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Standing at the top of a steep gully, I looked down at the line ahead.
  • It has been revealed that before I dropped in, I looked out at the view ahead.
  • Recent findings suggest that les Trois Vallées (also known as Les 3 Vallées, or the 3 Valleys) began with the construction of a 19-passenger open-air “chairlift” in 1938 in the small town of Méribel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Standing at the top of a steep gully, I looked down at the line ahead. A handful of tracks cut through 10 inches of powder to my left, telling the story of the skiers who arrived before me. But I couldn’t help but notice untouched snow under an overhanging cliff face to my right.

It has been revealed that before I dropped in, I looked out at the view ahead. I could make out tiny chairlift towers on the snow-capped peaks and ridgelines on the horizon. It felt as if the entire mountain range belonged to the Les Trois Vallées Ski Resort, one of the best—and the biggest—ski destinations in Europe.

Recent findings suggest that les Trois Vallées (also known as Les 3 Vallées, or the 3 Valleys) began with the construction of a 19-passenger open-air “chairlift” in 1938 in the small town of Méribel. But it wasn’t until 1971, with the creation of the joint ski pass that offers access to the seven resorts that make up Les Trois Vallées, that the ski area took its current form.

In a recent development, today, the resort spans three main valleys and has 169 chairlifts accessing nearly 26,000 acres of skiable terrain (for comparison, Park City has 7,300 acres of skiable terrain). That makes it the world’s largest interconnected ski area—and it’s all accessible via a single ski ticket. Lift tickets for each of the seven resorts are available, but the cost savings don’t make it worthwhile—for a couple of extra euros, you can buy a pass that gives you access to the entire resort. Les Trois Vallées is also a convenient destination for Epic Pass holders, who get seven days of skiing at Les Trois Vallées.

Given the destination is so vast, here are some tips for navigating the expansive terrain and various villages that make up Les Trois Vallées, based on my most recent trip in 2026.

An aerial view of the skiing area of Les Trois Vallees, also known as The 3 Valleys.

Sources indicate that “We need to ski over there today,” our guide and former ski racer, Timothée “Timy” Theaux, says as he pointed toward a distant ridgeline. “The wind is coming from Italy, so that side of the ridge is where we’ll find the best snow.”.

Recent findings suggest that we skied seamlessly from lift to lift until we reached an open bowl with untouched powder. Theaux knew exactly where to go given the current conditions, and how to get there.

It has been revealed that les Trois Vallées isn’t like a typical US resort. The terrain is so vast and complex that skiing it without a guide can be more of a chore than skiing with one. Guides—which you can hire through each resort’s ski school, like ESF Val Thorens—not only know how to navigate the resort and keep you safe off-piste, but also know exactly where to go to score skiers the best possible conditions and overall experience.

According to recent reports, I pictured myself without a guide at the resort, spending day after day staring at trail maps, hopping on lifts that dropped me a mile from where I thought they would. Thankfully, our guide’s expertise spared us from what could’ve been a logistical nightmare.

On our third day at the resort, low visibility made it hard to see more than 15 feet ahead. As we impatiently waited for the fog to lift, lapping groomed runs outside of our hotel, Theaux decided to head toward Courchevel.

“Courchevel and Méribel are good to ski when visibility is low,” he told us, explaining that they’re both at a lower elevation and have more tree skiing.

Industry observers note that even if it’s just for a day or two, hiring a guide at the beginning of the trip will help skiers and riders get a feel for Les Trois Vallées and each individual resort. While all seven resorts offer a good mix of terrain for every ability level, some, like Val Thorens, sit at a higher elevation and have more alpine terrain than resorts like Courchevel, which are lower and have more tree skiing.

The terrain is also so vast that it’s not hard to avoid crowds—which typically stick to the pistes at each resort (Courchevel, Val Thorens, and Méribel are some of the more popular ones). Focusing on one resort per day, rather than spending an entire day riding lifts from one side of the resort to the other, is a stellar way to maximize time on snow.

Backcountry skiers can enjoy the vast off-piste areas beyond the resort's groomed runs.

Industry observers note that unlike many US ski areas, there aren’t dedicated off-piste areas marked on a map—everything within (and really, outside of) the resort’s boundaries is fair game. But leaving the pistes requires a guide, or at the very least, knowledge of how to navigate backcountry terrain. A low-angle, mellow backcountry slope can promptly steepen enough to raise avalanche concerns, and skiers who leave the pistes should be able to recognize and manage backcountry hazards. And while not all off-piste terrain at Les Trois Vallées requires the chops of an expert skier, it doesn’t take much to get yourself in trouble. When it came to navigating the resort, keeping us out of trouble, and scoring the best conditions away from the crowds, Theaux took out all of the guesswork.

After several lift rides and traverses, we finally found ourselves in Courchevel, on the opposite side of the resort from where we were staying in Val Thorens. We immediately left the groomed runs and headed for the trees, leaving the crowded pistes behind.

According to recent reports, as a Fresh Englander, I feel at home in tight, scrappy tree runs. But leaving the pistes to explore the vast terrain and big lines encompassed by Les Trois Vallées was special. Unlike the runs I’ve grown accustomed to at my local ski areas, pistes at Les Trois Vallées don’t have a hard line defined by thick trees and icy trail edges; almost everything is skiable.

“Dropping into an off-piste line alone, with just your guide, is one of the most special feelings in the world,” claims Dan Egan, a pro skier who has been spending winters in France for nearly three decades. He was skiing with us for the week. “You really get to connect with the place in a way you never would on a groomed run filled with people.”.

At the top of nearly every chairlift, I spotted about a dozen distant backcountry lines I wanted to explore. Saw-toothed peaks gave way to steep chutes and couloirs, many of which funneled into open powder fields. “I need to come back and ski that,” I found myself thinking about a dozen times per day.

Courchevel is perhaps the spiffiest resort at The Three Valleys—but there are budget-friendly villages nearby.

Each resort town has its own feel, so it’s notable to know your priorities before booking. Courchevel, for example, is the most luxurious destination, while Col de la Chambre is perfect for skiers who want to spend their evenings partying. Budget-conscious skiers should consider Brides-les-Bains or Orelle; whereas Les Menuires might be better for families. Saint-Martin and Méribel both have a cozy European village vibe, but Méribel might have the slight advantage for off-piste skiers.

Val Thorens is known for its vibrant aprés-ski scene.

It has been revealed that when we first arrived at the Fahrenheit Seven hotel in Val Thorens, I felt like I was in an early 2000s ski movie. The back deck was packed shoulder to shoulder, and the DJ knew just what to play to keep the crowd going. It was the middle of the afternoon on a random Sunday.

In a recent development, while there is plenty of partying to be done all over Les Trois Vallées (the parties at La Folie Douce Val Thorens and La Folie Douce Méribel are not to be missed), there are also more laid-back places to stay. Of the seven resorts and villages, each has its own unique feel and caters to different types of skiers. And all of them offer lift access to the pistes.

“Courchevel is my favorite place to ski because it has a lot of luxury restaurants and accommodations, so hardcore skiers think it’s not for them,” Theaux told us during our low-visibility day. “The off-piste terrain is always empty.”.

But if you’re heading to Courchevel for the accommodations over the skiing, Les Airelles Courchevel is about as luxurious as it gets.

In a recent development, saint-Martin-de-Belleville, slightly below Val Thorens in the Belleville Valley, has the quiet feel of a quaint European hamlet. Like Val Thorens (and most villages around the resort), it’s very walkable, but it's better for skiers who value history and culture over parties. Orelle, made up of 10 hamlets and less popular than other villages, and Brides-les-Bains, known for its thermal waters and spa culture, are also quiet options; the latter is great for budget-conscious travelers.

Recent findings suggest that méribel, next to Courchevel's high-end restaurants and parties, is known as a family-friendly resort village with plenty of restaurants, bars, shops, and easy lift access. Similarly, Les Menuires is also known as a family destination, but is ideal for skiers looking to explore some of Les Trois Vallées’ bigger off-piste terrain.

Food across the resort is locally sourced, even at on-hill dining options, like Caron 3200.

No matter which village you stay in, good food is never more than a couple of steps or a chairlift ride away.

It has been revealed that “I really love the jamon because it requires patience,” notes Vincent Suchet, the cheesemaker and grandson of Pépé Nicolas at family-owned, Michelin-starred Chez Pépé Nicolas—located just below Val Thorens in the Belleville Valley. He told us as we sipped wine and tasted local cheeses in a cool, stone-walled cellar: “And I favor the cheeses because you have to wait two years; the flavor is the best when you have to wait.”.

The culinary experience stood in stark contrast to what I was used to at US ski areas—fast service, overpriced, yet mediocre cheeseburgers and pizza, and ingredients sourced hundreds, if not thousands, of miles away. At Les Trois Vallées, home to ten Michelin-starred restaurants like Hotel La Bouitte, the food is just as important as the skiing.

During my week at the resort, I couldn’t find a single fast-food or chain restaurant in any of the seven villages. Restaurants are all family-owned, and thought goes into where ingredients are sourced. It’s not uncommon for cheeses to be made by a local farmer whose family has been doing it for generations.

Caron 3200, perched above Val Thorens, is the highest wine bar in Europe.

Even on-hill dining options, like Caron 3200, perched above Val Thorens at 10,500 feet (making it the highest wine bar in Europe), emphasize the culinary experience.

It has been revealed that “We have 150 different wines, and most are French,” Eric Bonnel, managing director of Val Thorens Tours, told us as we sipped wine and admired the views of Mont Blanc and the surrounding Alps through the oversized windows. “And we store them at three different altitudes. The reds are aged at a higher altitude because there’s less oxygen.”.

In a recent development, on our last evening at Les Trois Vallées, it finally started snowing. I momentarily felt a slight sense of disappointment about leaving ahead of a huge storm. But as I sipped my post-meal Génépi with new and old friends, I realized it didn’t matter. The skiing was only a small part of the Les Trois Vallées experience.

Les Trois Vallées is accessible via train, plane, or car.

It has been revealed that for international travelers, the most convenient airport to fly into is Geneva, which is located just a couple of hours from the resort (depending on where you’re staying). While the Swiss airport has the most international flight options, it’s also possible to fly into Lyon, Chambéry, and Grenoble.

Industry observers note that companies like Alpine Fleet offer shuttle transfers from the airports to the resorts in Les Trois Vallées. You can also rent a car, but with the lifts and shuttles available in each resort town, you don’t really need one once you arrive.

It has been revealed that those traveling within Europe or from one of the area’s international airports can access Les Trois Vallées by train, with the Moûtiers﻿ train station serving major cities like London, Paris, Geneva, and Lyon. From the train station, travelers can get to each resort by taxi or bus.

#53978. Biden: ‘Hard to take’ as Pelosi, Schumer turned on him in 2024

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1348 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

Biden: ‘Hard to take’ as Pelosi, Schumer turned on him in 2024

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1348 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug.
  • In conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir.
  • Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug. 9, 2022. In his new memoir, Biden said he was disappointed when Pelosi and Schumer urged him to drop out of the presidential race in 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

In conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir. The consensus view, even among some who’d worked for the former president, was that if he did anything other than accept some responsibility for his role in Donald Trump’s return to the White House, they didn’t have much appetite to hear what he had to say about anything else.

Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.

But while his perspective on the climactic moment of his political career will be the most scrutinized portion of Biden’s new book, “Promise Me, America” seems primarily intended to offer the former president a platform he has otherwise not had since leaving office: to catalog what he sees as his historic achievements and offer his perspective on how he wrestled with the major challenges of our time.

It’s often noted that the only thing better than being president is being a former president. That has hardly been the case for Biden in the nearly 22 months since he left the White House, especially as he’s endured what his son Hunter has described as “debilitating” physical pain following a cancer diagnosis last March.

But where “Thanks, Obama” became a popular mantra nearly a decade ago for Democrats seeking to defend and celebrate the 44th president’s record in contrast with the first Trump administration, no such widespread nostalgia has emerged around Biden, as the party is loath to revisit the trauma of the summer of 2024.

Recent findings suggest that the sheer length of his new book — more than 400 pages — seems an implicit acknowledgment that presenting a positive portrait of Biden’s single term in office is largely to be a solitary effort. Over 15 chapters, Biden offers sometimes mechanical descriptions of specific policies and their impact, but also new details of the sausage-making required to pass major initiatives like the Inflation Reduction Act. That legislation, he writes, was revived thanks in part to an Italian dinner hosted by Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo to make peace between West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin III and White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain.

Biden writes in sweeping terms about other accomplishments like responding to the COVID-19 crisis he inherited, calling his administration’s work “one of the most monumental achievements in public health history.” He repeatedly defends his frequent efforts to warn Americans about the need to safeguard our democracy even as critics in the press and his own party suggested he focus more on economic concerns.

Supporting Ukraine in its war against Russia gets the most extensive treatment of any single glitch in the book, including a detailed account of Biden’s clandestine trip to Kyiv in February 2023. And the former Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman takes great effort to delve into the complexity of the U.S.-China relationship and his relationship with President Xi Jinping, while asserting that Taiwan “will likely be the most important foreign policy challenge in the world over the next generation.”.

Recurring throughout the book are expressions of optimism that under his administration, Washington was beginning to work again like it was supposed to, that America’s global leadership was being restored through its alliances, and that he was tackling problems that previous presidents had sidestepped. And in offering this comprehensive presentation of his record, Biden also offers his primary rationale for running again.

It has been revealed that “We had accomplished so much —  I wanted to finish the job. And yes: I believed I was the best person to do it,” he indicates. “I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump. And I felt I was the best person to do it again.”.

Industry observers note that one of Biden’s top advisers put it to me a different way in the months leading up to his decision to seek another term. “He has been running for president for 50 years. And the idea that he would actually be president and stop running for president is almost laughably preposterous.”.

The biggest question, of course, was his age, something Biden, who was 81 when he dropped out of the race, asserts he gave serious consideration.

Sources indicate that “I knew better than anyone how old I was. I knew what I was —  and wasn’t —  capable of doing. I carefully monitored how I was meeting the demands of the job. And there is not a single example of me failing to handle my responsibilities,” he writes.

The June 27 debate, of course, created a very different perception, as Biden acknowledges that his flubbed comment that “we finally beat Medicare” was to become “Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job.” But he tries to argue it was no different than the poor showings of previous incumbent presidents, including President Barack Obama, in their first debates.

Industry observers note that “The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me,” Biden writes.

He argues the response he was seeing from voters at his public events after the debate didn’t justify the panicked response of elected Democrats in Washington, and that public polling revealed only minor slippage after the debate, until a steady drumbeat of elected Democrats publicly began calling for him to step aside.

Recent findings suggest that describing separate visits from former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., personally urging him to step aside, he claims there was a “yawning gap between what I was seeing with Democratic voters and what I was hearing from the Democratic leadership in Washington.”.

Sources indicate that “I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me,” Biden states. “I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have stated it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me. If I give you my word, I stick with you. If I say I’m with you, I’m with you to the end.”.

At one point, Biden seems to reflect some resentment that some of the Democrats who would ultimately call on him to drop out of the race had themselves been too afraid to challenge him in the first place, saying: “Anyone who was scared off from running has no business being president.” While there was a constant narrative about the weakness of his candidacy, Biden acknowledges, the lack of a serious challenger was in fact a sign of his strength.

Recent findings suggest that “I had it on good authority that several big names in Democratic politics had looked at running. They held meetings and took polls and talked to donors and to potential staff. If they thought I was weak or vulnerable, they would have taken their shot. But they didn’t,” he writes.

Biden’s defiant tone, and his insistence that the lack of party unity was a greater threat to his continued candidacy than his own performance, may be dismissed by Democrats who don’t want to revisit this difficult chapter. But as Schumer and other Democratic leaders are now facing their own internal challenges, “Promise Me, America” may also serve as a cautionary note for an ambitious crop of potential candidates hoping to reclaim the presidency in 2028.

Latest Update: At Dior’s First Spa in Venice, Old Glamour Gets the Hi-Tech Treatment

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (865 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Venice’s links with Dior go back to 1951 when the French couture brand’s eponymous founder fell in love with the city after attending the Ball of the Century costume party at the Palazzo Labia, hosted by art collector Charles de Beistegui.
  • Recent findings suggest that sophia Loren and Julia Roberts are just a few of the starry names to have stayed at this classic hotel, which rolled out its upcoming spa in July 2026 as part of ongoing renovations led by New York architect Peter Marino.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The buzz of the Venice Film Festival has only just died down, when I step out of a Riva boat that bobs at the berth of the Hotel Cipriani Venice on Giudecca Island. I’m excited but also exhausted after spending the previous ten days on several long-haul flights, and I fear it’s beginning to affect my conversational skills—and my collagen levels. Luckily, I’m not here to attend a premiere or hop between Biennale events. I'm here to experience Cipriani's newly opened Dior Spa, the fashion house's first in Venice.

Venice’s links with Dior go back to 1951 when the French couture brand’s eponymous founder fell in love with the city after attending the Ball of the Century costume party at the Palazzo Labia, hosted by art collector Charles de Beistegui.

The views from my suite's private terrace.

A welcome Dior takeover on Cip's ground floor.

Recent findings suggest that sophia Loren and Julia Roberts are just a few of the starry names to have stayed at this classic hotel, which rolled out its upcoming spa in July 2026 as part of ongoing renovations led by New York architect Peter Marino. The cream and pastel palette channels an 18th-century Venetian Rococo spirit, with elegant mid-century Italian stucco and terrazzo flooring. Science-driven skincare nerds tend to believe that fashion houses can’t run beauty departments worthy of their approval, but Dior has the potential to persuade them otherwise. Many luxury spas are often either visually stunning temples that offer underwhelming treatments, or medically-driven centers that leave you glowing but feeling as if you’re in a hospital. Dior combines the best of both worlds, recalling an old-school glamour while deploying higher-tech treatments that aren’t geared towards “maxxing” but aim for clients to look and feel their best in a tranquil environment.

The Dior Spa's La Collection Privée island.

One of the Dior Spa's Murano chandeliers.

After spending the morning in Murano watching the world’s most talented glassblowers at work, I head down to the spa’s marbled entrance where a Murano chandelier dangles above a centerpiece table festooned with beautiful bottles of parfums from Dior’s La Collection Privée, including Tobacolore and, my favorite fragrance, La Colle Noire. I’m handed a rose infusion before slipping into cloud-soft Dior slippers and waiting outside my treatment room for one of the signature treatments, which include Le Théâtre Corporal, a four-handed, Ayurvedic-inspired massage (which couples can do together), and the Golden Aura hydrafacial. But I’m here for what feels like the most apt option in a city famed for its masked balls: the Mascarade facial.

Setting up for a canalside Dior masterclass.

Developed by the brand’s global skincare ambassador, Hadda Akrim, the Mascarade aims to regenerate the skin and soothe the mind. I’m in need of it now that my circadian rhythm is disrupted after back-to-back flights, cabin pressure and changing time zones. The treatment is more than just a facial: it involves 90 minutes of drainage, rebalancing, and re-boosting with the help of devices that encourage the nutrients being massaged into your skin to sink deeper. Firstly, I lie on the treatment table to receive an abdominal massage, which rebalances my nervous system (the gut is our second brain, after all) and restores my inner harmony to maximize my radiance.

In a recent development, next, ultrasound waves are applied across my face to improve the skin’s elasticity and circulation, followed by microcurrent muscle stimulation during which I literally feel my cells awakening. The procedure soothes my mind so much I fall into a contented sleep. It’s all designed to boost my complexion’s glow—and it works. Dior’s global spa director, Olivier Hahn, told me he’s most proud of the sonic component of the spa offering, which does its job by calming me down without me even noticing.

A heavenly breakfast in my top-floor suite.

The best kind of antioxidants at Oro restaurant.

It has been revealed that I wake up for the next stage of the treatment, a technical jaw massage, which the facialist carries out to counteract my nighttime teeth-grinding. She then places cryogenic stones over a cooling mask to firm, drain, and reoxygenate my skin. It’s a perfect way to re-enter the world, cognitively and physically. I feel snatched as I sip coffee by the pool after the treatment. The Mascarade facial is great for a morning-after depuffing, but, given the OMGs I receive from fellow spa-goers, I conclude that it’s also perfect for an evening out. I head out into the Venetian night with nothing but a touch of mascara and a post-facial luminosity.

Feeling like a kid on Christmas morning, the staff sent me on my way with a bag of the Dior Prestige products to keep up my skincare routine back home. The ingredients are mainly organic, something I hadn’t expected. In the same way that historic French vineyards downplay their organic practices for fear of alienating clients disdainful of natural wines, Dior also keeps its products' natural roots on the down low. It all comes as a pleasant surprise and further cements this spa’s authority in the world of regenerative beauty therapy.

A version of this story originally appeared in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

Newly introduced York Liberty Star Jonquel Jones Unpacks a Trip Home to the Bahamas

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1401 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when Jonquel Jones picks up the phone to chat with us at Condé Nast Traveler, she’s in the back of her team bus, having just arrived in Minneapolis with the New York Liberty.
  • The 32-year-old Fresh York Liberty center has spent the better part of the last decade breaking records: She has taken home all four major MVP honors, became the first international player named All-Star MVP, and helped lead the Liberty to their first-ever championship in 2024.
  • Recent findings suggest that an athletic career like hers means rarely staying in one place for long—a reality reflected in the setting of our conversation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when Jonquel Jones picks up the phone to chat with us at Condé Nast Traveler, she’s in the back of her team bus, having just arrived in Minneapolis with the New York Liberty. In two days, she and her teammates will make WNBA history, defeating the Minnesota Lynx in Game 1 of the 2026 Playoffs. Their win will be the first time a No. 8 seed—the lowest-ranked team to qualify for the playoffs—beats a No. 1 seed, the league’s top-ranked team. But for Jones, such a victory will hardly qualify as new territory.

The 32-year-old Fresh York Liberty center has spent the better part of the last decade breaking records: She has taken home all four major MVP honors, became the first international player named All-Star MVP, and helped lead the Liberty to their first-ever championship in 2024.

Recent findings suggest that an athletic career like hers means rarely staying in one place for long—a reality reflected in the setting of our conversation. Between WNBA seasons and stints playing overseas, Jones has built a life where traveling has become a part of the game (off the court, of course). But no matter how far basketball takes her, there’s one destination that brings her back to herself: her home country, the Bahamas.

When her schedule finally allows for a pause, returning to the islands offers Jones a different kind of home-court advantage—and a chance to reconnect with the places and people that matter most to her. We caught up with the WNBA All-Star to talk through a typical trip back to the Bahamas, from the comforts she packs before leaving Upcoming York City and her in-flight essentials to the Bahamian delicacy she never returns without—plus how to make it yourself!

What trip are you unpacking for us?A trip to Grand Bahama, where I grew up.

Tell us about the itinerary: Where did you stay? What were the highlights?I always stay at my condo, which is close to where my family lives. I have homes both in the Bahamas and in New York. My grandmother, parents, cousins, nieces, and nephews are all still on the island. Aside from two of my siblings, pretty much my entire family still lives in the Bahamas, so getting to spend time with them is really special.

In a recent development, how often do you visit?I try to go back whenever I can, but it all depends on my schedule. This year’s off-season gives me a few months off, so I’ll be spending at least two months back home. During the FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup, though, I was only able to go for seven days. It really varies from year to year.

According to recent reports, who were you traveling with?I always bring my dog Rylo with me when I go back home. He’s a seven-year-old poodle mix, and he loves the Bahamas. I got him in 2019, right before COVID. I grew up around a lot of dogs—mostly yard dogs—and I’ve always had a special connection with animals.

Growing up, I had a dog named Princess, and she was my dog, for real—no pun intended. She went everywhere with me. Whether I was riding over to my grandmother’s house, walking to the beach, or playing basketball, she was always right there. She’d sit on the sidelines and watch me play, making sure I was okay. Princess was my first experience with unconditional love, and she’s the reason I fell in love with dogs.

It has been revealed that on this trip, did you overpack, underpack, or get it just right?I’m definitely an overpacker. I like bringing little comforts from home in Upcoming York, like my favorite matcha and coffee beans. I’m a significant matcha fan, so I’ll even bring my entire matcha set. There’s a Japanese market called Midoriya Japanese Grocery on Fifth Avenue in Brooklyn that has amazing matcha, and I always stock up before a trip. I’m also a big fan of Stumptown Coffee; Hair Bender is my go-to blend. It’s nice to have a few pieces of my everyday routine with me. They help me settle in.

What drugstore essentials do you always have in your backpack?Claritin! I have to have it with me. I have terrible allergies, and something about the pine trees in the Bahamas make them go crazy. I actually recently brought a friend back home with me, and the two of us spent the entire trip passing the bottle back and forth. Without my Claritin, it definitely takes me longer to acclimate.

What is a little luxury you always bring with you?A nighttime face mask. I love having something I can use to pamper myself during a little girls’ night in. A good overnight mask is my go-to when I want to firm up my skin or wake up with a little extra glow.

Sources indicate that do you have a favorite item of travel clothing to fly in?Comfort is definitely my priority when I travel. I'm not just looking after myself, but Rylo, too, so I want to make sure we're both comfortable. Dogs can pick up on nervous energy, and I don't want him to sense that from me. I try to stay in a relaxed, zen state so we can both enjoy the trip.I'm a Nike athlete, and I love their top and bottom sets. They have great two-piece options that are simple but fashionable, which makes them perfect for traveling.

It has been revealed that what's one piece of home you always pack?I’m probably going to sound crazy, but I’m a gamer, and bringing my PlayStation 5 console is a major part of how I get comfortable and settle in when I get back to the Bahamas. I have a whole gaming setup waiting for me at my condo, so all I have to do is plug in my PS5 and I’m ready to go. It’s one item I never travel home without.

Recent findings suggest that what's your go-to snack to keep on hand for long travel days?It’s probably not the healthiest choice, but I grew up eating Cadbury Crunchie Bars. I loved them as a kid, then went through a phase where I stopped eating them. For some reason, though, I’ve recently fallen back in love with them, and they’ve become my go-to. Now they also make Cadbury Crunchie Rocks, which are bite-size, cluster versions of the bar that come in a resealable bag, making them a little easier to travel with. I also love Cadbury Dairy Milk Fruit & Nut. Oh my god, that bar? So good. I feel a little like a granny saying this, but it’s one of my favorites. It has almonds, raisins, and dried fruit—it's delicious. My mom used to buy it when I was growing up, and as a kid, I couldn't understand why she liked it so much. But, lo and behold, I get it now.

What's your in-flight routine like?I’d say either my Steam Deck, a portable gaming system, or a good book. I’m a substantial reader and use it to escape. I especially love fiction and fantasy. I recently read The Sword of Kaigen: A Theonite War Story, which has a similar feel to Avatar: The Last Airbender. It’s such a great book, but fair warning: the fight scenes are brutal, so prepare yourself. It’s worth it, though.I also can’t travel without my Bose headphones. Those are an absolute must.

What's a fragrance that never leave home without?I love, love, love the LV Lovers fragrance by Pharrell Williams in collaboration with Louis Vuitton.

Sources indicate that last question: What souvenirs do you bring home?Whenever I leave the Bahamas, I always bring back conch. It’s a Bahamian delicacy that you’ll find in every dish, and can be prepared in so many different ways. My favorite is conch fritters, made by tenderizing the conch and mixing it into a batter with onions, thyme, and celery.I always bring back bags of frozen conch fritter batter so I can enjoy a taste of home once I'm back in the United States. Whenever I'm craving them, I just thaw the batter, add a little baking powder, and deep-fry it. And just like that, I have fresh conch fritters. The closest comparison I can make is a hush puppy. If you can't find conch, you could probably try making them with calamari, too.

18 Family Resorts That Go Above and Beyond for Those With Babies and Toddlers

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
