11 Best Airbnbs in Stockholm for Historic Architecture, Saunas, and Beach Access

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For a break that balances the buzz of discovering a newly introduced city with a good dose of fresh air, Stockholm’s mix of lush parks and eclectic architecture is an enduring choice.
  • These 11 excellent rentals throughout the city and its outskirts balance top-notch amenities with the freedom that only comes with a private booking.
  • We've vetted these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For a break that balances the buzz of discovering a newly introduced city with a good dose of fresh air, Stockholm’s mix of lush parks and eclectic architecture is an enduring choice. The city is formed of 14 islands, meaning you’re never too far from a waterfront to amble along. It's packed with historical charm (head to Gamla Stan to see one of Europe’s oldest medieval cobbled streets), as well as stylish boutiques and museums championing everything from Abba to the world’s best-preserved 17th-century warship. While the city is home to a slew of excellent hotels, from elegant converted townhouses to the former home of Astrid Lindgren (author of the beloved Pippi Longstocking book series), you’ll want to look to Airbnb for a real home-from-home vibe.

These 11 excellent rentals throughout the city and its outskirts balance top-notch amenities with the freedom that only comes with a private booking. True to Nordic form, there’s a clutch of homes with their own sauna and steam rooms, and all have either sea or skyline views. Below, the best Airbnbs in Stockholm to book for a weekend of weaving through medieval streets, gallery hopping, and lots of cinnamon buns.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Historic architecture, prime location, dedicated workspace.

In a recent development, subverting traditional Scandi minimalist sensibilities, this cool retreat in the hip heart of Södermalm channels a moody, more underground kind of charm. On the top floor, light-flooded, open-strategy living areas are packed with rich, creamy furnishings and crisp architectural lines—multiple previous guests say that this is one of the most stylish homes they’ve ever stayed in. Downstairs, two tranquil bedrooms are carved directly into the exposed natural rock, so you can sleep beneath historic vaulted ceilings after a long day skipping from sight to sight. On that note: Södermalm is an eclectic area of town, with plenty of vintage shops and wine bars, after which you can hole up in this cocooning, cave-like retreat, as though you’re stepping into your own secret—and very stylish—bunker.

Neighborhood: SödermalmThings to do nearby: Fotografiska, Riddarholm Church, Stockholm City Museum.

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Forest access, indoor fireplace, outdoor gas grill.

Blink, and you might miss this off-grid, A-frame cabin, hidden among a thick swathe of pine trees. It’s worth searching for: Once you make your way through the foliage, you’ll find a truly wonderful Swedish escape for two. The glass-fronted structure invites in all of the elements, while inside, it’s time to switch off—there’s a crackling open hearth where you can grill all of your meals, and precious little noise other than the rustle of wind through the canopy. Fair warning: There’s a very rustic toilet and seasonal shower about a 30-second walk down the forest path, so if you’re not a DIY fan, perhaps look elsewhere. Nonetheless, for more adventurous sorts, the trade-off means absolute tranquility surrounded by happily grazing sheep and twinkly starry night skies—all within a hop and a skip of the capital.

Neighborhood: VärmdöThings to do nearby: Lillsved Beach, Buddharama Temple, Stora Sandön.

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Historic warehouse, steps from the lake, wood-burning fireplace.

It has been revealed that wood-beamed ceilings, clattering floors, a muted color scheme, and a signature bright exterior welcome you in from the cold—this former warehouse just oozes 19th-century charm the moment you round the corner. Better yet, it’s totally massive, sprawling across three roomy floors, with a prime spot perched right on the peaceful banks of Åkers canal. A snazzy and social kitchen space opens onto a central island and a fireplace, where all the family will want to gather. When it’s time to bed down, there are cozy curtained sleeping nooks and an additional attic dormitory, adding a playful, rustic vibe. You can rent canoes from host Cecile to paddle down the canal, or jump on an e-bike to explore the surrounding nature reserves. When you return, fire up the outdoor grill and gather around the dining table for a long dinner with more endless views.

Neighborhood: Norrö-StavaThings to do nearby: Prästfjärden lake, Näsudden nature reserve, Åkersbro walking trails.

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Sea views, sauna, hot tub.

In a recent development, this joyfully bobbing houseboat turns the gray blue waters of the Baltic into something akin to your own front lawn—and it does so just 15 minutes from the heady sights of central Stockholm. Panoramic floor-to-ceiling glass means you feel that you’re virtually out on the water—and, of course, you can dive straight into the lake from your bedroom deck. Dry off and hop into the private wood-fired sauna to warm up. Hop off the boat, and you can sunbathe on the jetty, cook up some local catches on the barbecue, or jump into the complimentary canoe. All in all, this is an idyllic waterside playground that active types will love.

Neighborhood: BooThings to do nearby: Kringelgården bakery, Saltsjöbadens golf course, Artipelag.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Sauna, beach access, pet-friendly.

According to recent reports, expect some truly good seascape ASMR when you stay here—you’re so close to the water you can hear the waves rolling onto the shore right from the porch. Grab the kayak from the cupboard and head down to the beach to make the most of this beautiful location. It’s a short drive from the home to Stockholm’s city center, but you’re rewarded with much serenity and glorious views instead. For those seeking a secluded family stay, this is the place.

Neighborhood: TyresöThings to do nearby: Sandholmarna nature preserve, Tyresta nature reserve, Lilla beach.

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Wood stove, sauna, beach access.

Industry observers note that this spacious waterside cottage is not in Stockholm’s city center, but by compromising on a 30-minute commute into town, you gain something really special. The owners took the original 130-year-old structure down piece by piece, rebuilding it on their own property. It was worth the effort. Now, it lies surrounded by pine trees in a nature reserve beside a sparkling, clear lake, with the sea just a few steps further in the other direction. A large porch provides the spot for barbecue dinners and sunbathing sessions in the summer, and there are two spas within walking distance for those looking for their Scandi sweat fix—the sea-facing Skepparholmen Spa, and Japanese onsen-style Yasuragi. But you don't have to head that far, as the property has its own sauna. Stay in as long as you can muster, then cool off by jumping in the lake—something all the more satisfactory in the winter months.

Neighborhood: BooThings to do nearby: Boobadet Beach, Nyckelvikens wildlife refuge, Sushi Bar Namiyama.

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Rooftop views, beach access, pet-friendly.

A previous guest indicates this flat has a Upcoming York City vibe, and we can see why—the interior space is small but stylish, with an industrial bent and views all over the coolest part of Stockholm from the balcony. It’s on the top floor of this apartment block, so the vistas can’t be beat. It’s been a winner for those on work trips, thanks to superfast WiFi and a dedicated workspace, and, unusually for Airbnb stays, you can bring your dog too.

Neighborhood: SödermalmThings to do nearby: Liljeholmsviken waterfront, Högalid Church, Skinnarviksberget.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathroomWhy we love it: Steam room, in-unit washer/dryer, fully equipped kitchen.

It has been revealed that for an Airbnb stay that’s as close to checking into a luxury hotel as possible, look to this plush apartment right in the city center. The whole place is brand new, and no expense has been spared on the fittings—there are genuine oak floorboards, Italian travertine surfaces, underfloor heating, and a slew of top-notch furniture, plus little touches such as a shower seat and a gloriously powerful rainfall shower. The best bit is the steam room; there’s no better way to decompress after a long flight or a blustery autumnal walk by the river.

Neighborhood: VasastanThings to do nearby: Vanadislunden park, Odenplan plaza, Swedish Museum of Natural History.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Proximity to metro, private patio, in-unit washer/dryer.

If dopamine itself could be characterized as a building, it’d be this one. The place (all 300 square feet of it) is pure joy from top to bottom—with a pink-tiled kitchen, mint-green bathroom, and cozy bedroom nook with yellow walls and blue candy-striped bedding. Cheery artworks add a final flourish. Despite its bijou size, there’s room for two more guests on the pullout bed, and there’s a patio with twinkly fairy lights to sit out on sunny afternoons with a book, a glass of wine, or both.

Neighborhood: ÄlvsjöThings to do nearby: Älvsjö Forest Nature Preserve, Herrängens Gård, Långbro park.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Beach access, sauna, kayak.

Forget your average homely fisherman’s cottage—this home here, on the cusp of the lake in the city’s swish Stocksund neighborhood, marks a newer, more modern breed of lake house. It’s chic as anything you’ll find in the city, with smooth, polished concrete floors and knotty pine walls finished with a moody, cocooning interior palette. Sweeping glass windows make the most of the beautiful views that stretch over the water and right to the city as it twinkles on the other side. Grab the kayak and spend an afternoon bobbing on the lake, then stop in for a well-deserved sweat session in the private sauna.

Neighborhood: StocksundThings to do nearby: Restaurang Hemma, Svanholmsparken park, Swedish Museum of Natural History.

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Wood-burning fireplace, Aesop toiletries, garden view.

This traditional Swedish apartment has had a modern facelift recently. Now it pairs gorgeous original features, including imposing 10-foot-high ceilings and whitewashed floorboards, with a sleek new kitchen and selection of cool designer furniture pieces. There's also a truly cloudlike sofa just made for cozy nights in. The surrounding streets are just as cool as the interiors; this home is smack dab in SoFo—by far Stockholm’s trendiest district—so you're just one street over from a clutch of the best of the city’s bar, restaurant, and café scene.

Neighborhood: SödermalmThings to do nearby: Fotografiska, Stockholm City Museum, Vitabergsparken park.

Hyatt Adds Stackable Awards, But Globalists Lose Free Parking Benefit

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1043 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that world of Hyatt is adding new Milestone Rewards and allowing members to combine awards starting in 2027.
  • In a recent development, hyatt has revealed changes beginning January 1, 2027, that will give members more ways to earn and redeem rewards.
  • Globalists right now receive complimentary parking on eligible award nights at participating hotels where parking can be charged to the room.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that world of Hyatt is adding new Milestone Rewards and allowing members to combine awards starting in 2027. There is plenty to like, particularly the ability to apply a suite upgrade to a free night certificate. But Globalists will lose automatic free parking on award stays, and a uniform one-year expiration will make some awards harder to use.

In a recent development, hyatt has revealed changes beginning January 1, 2027, that will give members more ways to earn and redeem rewards. But there are concessions here too, especially for frequent guests who already make good use of the existing benefits.

Let’s start with the parking change.

Globalists right now receive complimentary parking on eligible award nights at participating hotels where parking can be charged to the room. That can be a substantial benefit, particularly at city hotels and resorts with expensive parking.

Hyatt is replacing that status benefit with a selectable Free Parking Award, first available at 60 qualifying nights or 100,000 Base Points. Each award will cover one qualifying stay of up to seven nights and can be gifted. The improvement is that the award will work on eligible paid stays too. The drawback is that members must select it instead of another reward.

Hyatt tells Live And Let’s Fly:.

“This decision was made as 70% of Globalists did not use the free parking benefit in 2025; 95% used it 4 times or less, and moving this to a choice allowed the program to retain it for members who value it and introduce other exciting upcoming awards like the $200 Thompson Hotels Credit and the $500 Premium Suite Credit.”.

After that, Globalist status alone will not provide free parking.

I appreciate the advance notice, but this is a devaluation for members who regularly drive to Hyatt properties and redeem points, a benefit I used regularly when I was still Globalist and still use on Guest of Honor awards today.

Sources indicate that the ability to stack eligible awards is the most appealing part of this announcement and is a very positive change. Starting in 2027, members can combine a Suite Upgrade Award with a free night certificate, including Category 1–4, Category 1–7, Ultimate Free Night, and other eligible promotional certificates.

That addresses a frustrating restriction and having both a free night and a suite upgrade in your account should make it easier to initiative a special stay. Other eligible combinations will include Suite Upgrade Awards, Guest of Honor Awards, and Free Parking Awards on the same reservation.

According to recent reports, for someone without Globalist status, combining a confirmed suite with Guest of Honor benefits could make for a very nice stay. For a Globalist, being able to confirm a suite while using a free night certificate is also very useful.

There are still restrictions. For example, the latest Thompson Hotels and Premium Suite credits cannot be combined with a Free Night Award (I address the new milestone awards below). Hyatt has published the details on its 2027 updates page.

Awards issued beginning January 1, 2027, will expire 365 days after issuance.

That makes the rules easier to remember, but whether it helps depends on the award.

In a recent development, some milestone free night certificates at the moment expire after 180 days. Doubling that window is welcome…six months can pass very quickly when you are trying to find the right opportunity to use a certificate.

According to recent reports, but Suite Upgrade Awards, Club Access Awards, and Guest of Honor Awards right now can remain valid considerably longer, through the end of February of the second calendar year after they are earned. Reducing those to one year is a loss. Even today as I look to book stays in January and February of next year, I’ll be using those “older” Guest of Honor Awards.

That said, I would not call this change unreasonable and for most people it will be a net positive.

Milestone Rewards will begin at 10 qualifying nights or 20,000 Base Points, with additional milestones every 10 nights through 150.

Here are some notable upcoming choices (which are in addition to the existing choices):.

The $500 Premium Suite Credit awarded at 100 nights requires an eligible paid stay of at least two nights. I would evaluate that against what I would otherwise spend…a discount on an expensive suite is only useful if you would not otherwise get the upgrade anyway as a Globalist.

There are other trade-offs worth noting.

At 50 nights, the suite upgrade choice drops from two awards to one.

At 60 nights, My Hyatt Concierge becomes a selection rather than an automatic benefit (a worthless benefit, in my opinion). Members will choose two rewards from a menu that also includes suite upgrades, parking, points, and a skimpy Delta eCertificate.

If you value your concierge and want to retain the suite upgrades, that leaves no selection for parking….

It has been revealed that the new Delta partnership adds eCertificates at milestones from 20–60 nights, two single-visit Sky Club passes at 70, 80, and 90 nights, and Medallion status options at higher thresholds. Of course the Delta Air Lines awards replace the American Airlines awards.

Members will need to link their Hyatt and Delta accounts. Hyatt is also enhancing “Pay My Way” so members can choose awards, points, cash, or Points + Cash for individual nights within a stay.

Hyatt’s technology has long lagged, but this is a nice new revision.

The ability to combine free night certificates with suite upgrades is an excellent change. Earlier milestones and additional reward choices should also give members more opportunities to find something useful.

But the parking change is a loss for Globalists who regularly use that benefit. Shorter validity for some awards, fewer suite upgrades at 50 nights, and making concierge access a choice deserve attention too, as much I always loathed my own concierge agents.

Sources indicate that I appreciate that Hyatt is providing notice and protecting existing parking benefits during the transition. All in all, I’d say these changes are positive, but will hurt some travelers a lot more than others.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After a lovely stay in Vienna, we continued our journey to Zürich onboard an Austrian Airlines A320 in economy class.

We arrived at the airport around 9:30 am, figuring there would be no need to get there early to use a lounge when we had just enjoyed an excellent breakfast at the Park Hyatt Vienna.

The airport was busy but we used the Star Gold corridor to enjoy expedited security and were soon at the gate, ready to board our short flight to Switzerland.

Stepping onboard, we headed to the back to find our seats in row 22.

The Austrian A320 has 180 seats arranged in a 3-3 configuration (same in business class, though the middle seat is blocked).

It has been revealed that the Recaro BL3520 “NEK” slimline seats are very uncomfortable with very little padding. These are familiar seats if you have flown within Europe on Lufthansa Group carriers, with a literature pocket and a folding tray table on the seatback ahead.

Recent findings suggest that legroom varies by aircraft and row. Austrian lists a minimum economy class seat pitch of just 28 inches across its A320 fleet, so do not expect much room to stretch out, though it felt like we had 29 inches.

According to recent reports, there are no power ports or USB ports on this aircraft. Thankfully, however, there are individual air vents, unlike on the 777.

In economy class, passengers receive a free glass of water and Austrian chocolate.

For those peckish, buy-on-board is available. I pre-ordered a hot meal from the carrier’s Austrian Melangerie menu.

Recent findings suggest that what else would I order on Austrian Airlines but Wiener Schnitzel? While a proper Wiener Schnitzel is made with veal, Austrian uses chicken onboard, describing the dish as:.

Golden-brown chicken schnitzel with parsley potatoes.

The price was €13.80, though I received a 10% discount for pre-ordering.

Industry observers note that presentation was very much like economy class: the schnitzel and potatoes were served together in a cardboard box, but sometimes you have to look beyond the presentation. The chicken was tender, the breading remained surprisingly crisp, and the parsley potatoes were a nice accompaniment…my son Augustine and I both enjoyed it.

I highlighted this meal in a recent Meal of the Week feature.

> Read More: Austrian Airlines’ €13.80 Wiener Schnitzel On An 80-Minute Flight.

Recent findings suggest that I had also hoped to try the Julius Meinl Wiener Melange, a €5.20 coffee served with milk foam in a proper ceramic cup on a silver tray. Alas, Austrian only offers the Melange on flights of at least 80 minutes and our Vienna to Zürich flight was apparently five minutes too short according to the flight attendant.

Before landing I used the lavatory in the rear of the aircraft and it was messy by that point, with paper towels overflowing from the waste receptacle.

In a recent development, while there is no seatback screens or streaming movies and TV highlights, Wi-Fi was available for purchase onboard. A high speed pass (Viasat) was 6€ while messaging was free. I had trouble connecting, initially, but ultimately was able to pay the 6€ and connect.

This was a quick, boring flight with a delicious lunch onboard thanks to the buy-on-board menu. I’d never go out of my way to fly Austrian shorthaul in economy class, but if you are stuck behind the curtain, do take advantage of the pre-order menu to make the flight go by a bit faster.

My original review, covering an Austrian Airlines A320 journey from Vienna to Yerevan, Armenian (fun trip!) in 2019 is below.

What is Austrian Airlines like on a mid-haul flight in economy class?

It has been revealed that my business partner, John, and I spent a weekend in Yerevan, Armenia last month. We were in Vienna earlier in the week, so the nonstop Austrian flight from VIE to EVN made the most sense. We booked for 15,000 United miles each in economy class.

Business class would have been an extra 10,000 miles, but I figured 1.) the seat is the same, 2.) I already had lounge access, and 3.) we would be eating dinner just before the flight. So the upgrade did not make sense.

Recent findings suggest that vienna International Airport is such an easy airport to navigate. Check-in (John had to check a bag), security, and passport control took only a few moments. I’ll review the Austrian lounge in a separate post.

Boarding commenced precisely on schedule with business class passenger and Star Alliance Gold members invited to board first.

Recent findings suggest that I’ll start with the seats and the following warning: these slimline seats are very uncomfortable. By the time we reached Yerevan three hours later, I could not wait to get off. The seats do recline slightly, but the lack of padding makes for an uncomfortable flying experience on flights longer than 60-90 minutes. But that’s hardly a unique experience to Austrian. Seat pitch is 30 inches.

Notice that the only difference in business class hard product is that the middle seat is blocked:.

Recent findings suggest that A sticker on the aircraft fuselage indicated wi-fi internet would be available, but it did not function. There are no in-seat power ports.

But Austrian does a few things right.

According to recent reports, first, I appreciated the pillows and blankets, both of which were better than many airlines offer in economy class. Heck, United does not even offer pillows in domestic first class except on premium transcontinental flight.

That said, it was roasting outside and the cabin was not overly cool…not exactly heavy blanket weather.

It has been revealed that second, I appreciated the meal, as small as it was. A vegetarian cheese pasta with cake and bread was served after takeoff. Talk about a load of carbs! Passengers were not offered a choice of meal.

Flight attendants came around before the meal and also about 90 minutes before landing with a beverage serevice.

Finally, the lavatory was very clean…these pictures are toward the end of the flight.

Sources indicate that I appreciate that Austrian is full service in the sense that blankets, pillows, and meals are provided. But three hours really pushes the limit for this type of slimline seat. I’ll happily fly Austrian again, but ideally on a shorthaul route or on a widebody jet in business class….

Latest aviation funding request hits Senate turbulence

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov.
  • Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.
  • Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., mentioned he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks with reporters on Nov. 10. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Republicans appeared skeptical Monday about the need for as much as $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s aging air traffic control system, after a nationwide ground stop last Friday prompted the massive, increased asking price from top administration officials.

Speaking with reporters, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., mentioned he believed the department still had about $8 billion outstanding from an air traffic control modernization package included in last year’s reconciliation law.

“I got to obviously see the explanation behind it, or sort of laying out the numbers why it's necessary,” Thune noted of the $50 billion, which jumped from $30 billion a day earlier.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters he was unimpressed by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s request and that he wanted to see a breakdown of how the department would use the funds.

“They got to give us an update,” Tillis noted. “I mean, the $50 billion request — I thought that was $30 billion. So people have got to explain to me, really, even the basis for the $30 billion, let alone the additional $20 billion that Duffy mentioned the other day.”.

Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., similarly said legislators would need “more detail” on the request but said “obviously there needs to be more” funding for the modernization efforts.

Hoeven serves on the Senate Transportation-HUD Appropriations Subcommittee, which rolled out a fiscal 2027 spending bill Monday that would increase the FAA’s annual allocation to facilities and equipment by $500 million, a nearly 13 percent boost.

It has been revealed that duffy is slotted to attend the Senate GOP conference lunch on Tuesday, where he is likely to be peppered with such requests for specifics. Meanwhile, FAA staff are expected to brief House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee aides on Tuesday, after that meeting got pushed on Monday.

The Senate’s go-slow approach is in contrast to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who said over the weekend that he would add the $50 billion request to a year-end legislative package.

It has been revealed that the White House’s call for additional funds ballooned last week in the aftermath of the nationwide ground stop that created confusion and concern at airports around the country. The Federal Aviation Administration said Sunday that the unusual move was made “out of an abundance of caution” after legacy equipment became flooded with data during routine upgrades.

The FAA’s initial investigation tied the data flooding to work being done at a radar site in Texas and a radio communications site in Arkansas by contractor L3Harris Technologies.

Speaking on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Duffy said the server thought to have caused the flooding was taken to the L3Harris lab in Florida where FAA personnel are working with the FBI to analyze the router that likely caused the system instability.

Still, as administration officials attempt to understand the system errors that led to the ground stop, Duffy has used the moment as justification to lobby for additional funds.

It has been revealed that “In this old telecom network, I do have money to switch over from the old copper wires to fiber and we’re 70 percent completed with that mission, but we need a brand fresh architecture for our telecom and aviation,” Duffy mentioned on CNBC Monday. “This can happen promptly to build a new state of the art telecom network, it’s just that it has to be funded.”.

A day before the incident, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought wrote to congressional appropriators, formally asking for $30.1 billion in added funds for the modernization effort, in line with a bill introduced by Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., in late September. That ask inexplicably jumped up to $50 billion by Friday night in the aftermath of the ground stop.

On Monday, Thune noted the prior request for approximately $30 billion, which he noted included “some other stuff” as well.

Schmitt’s bill and the White House request would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $7.2 billion for a “common automation platform and a common controller workstation,” and $2 billion for cloud computing and telecommunications infrastructure.

Another $10 billion would go toward airport improvement projects, including $2 billion to “construct, replace, and improve terminal air traffic control facilities, including activities using digital tower technologies.”.

The request includes $10 billion for a terminal modernization or reconstruction pilot program for certain midsized airports.

Thune stated Monday that he tallied about $12 billion in the latest request specifically for air traffic control related concerns, likely a reference to the $10.1 billion plus the $2 billion for terminal facilities.

“I think there's more we need to figure out, and obviously I think we all agree that we need to be modernizing and updating, particularly in an area like that where safety is the number one priority, but also we want to do that in a smart way and make sure that we're using taxpayer dollars wisely and well,” Thune remarked. “We’ll hear him out.”.

Meanwhile, Democrats kept up the drumbeat of criticism, both for the airspace management that led to the ground stop and the rollout of the latest funding request.

Sources indicate that “So typical of this incompetent administration — they have money, they don’t use it and then they come back and say ‘give us more money,'” Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., remarked on the floor.

Savannah Behrmann and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is my fourth year leading our guide to the Best Places to Go in Central and South America, and each time I’m in awe of the final result—our list for 2027 is no exception. We’re talking about a region where the Pacific, the Atlantic, and the Caribbean converge; where the Andes reach for the Amazon; and where strings of puffy volcanoes and postcard-worthy islands stud the map like jewels. Within it all there are thriving cities where cultures ancient and modern collide head-on, and small towns that are timeless in a way that feels increasingly rare.

It may be a fool’s errand to distill all this wonder into a list of just 10 destinations. But the places below, as singular or more broadly representative as they may be, are the region’s answer to how we are traveling right now. For example, a pioneering set of travel specialists are ready to bring you to eco-lodges that are tucked in the untamed jungle of Guyana for wildlife sightings and citizen science experiences that will broaden your understanding of the only (official) English-speaking country in South America. If you’re looking for a sport to pick up, Preá on Brazil’s northeast coast has an open invitation on kitesurfing, the wind-driven sport this fishing village has long been known for—and the reason a set of quietly luxurious boutique hotels have been cropping up within driving distance of the rolling sand dunes of Jericoacoara National Park. If wine is what moves you, then Chile’s Central Valley should be your next stop: A slew of newly introduced culinary experiences and interesting bottles from up-and-coming winemakers make this Santiago-adjacent region the trip to take in 2027. There’s also next-gen wellness in Costa Rica, quintessential expedition cruises in Ecuador, offseason trekking in Argentina, and so much more.

Get ready to max out that PTO. These are the Best Places to Go in Central and South America in 2027. —Megan Spurrell.

This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here.

Go for: new jungle stays, ancestral wellness experiences, and a next-level approach to ecotourism.

Tucked in the Monteverde Cloud Forest, Hotel Belmar's Artista Villages offers 10 bungalows in a reforestation site.

The chance to connect with nature has long been a draw to this region—at Hotel Belmar, that includes activities like yoga.

Half a century ago Costa Rica helped pioneer a new model of travel in the Monteverde Cloud Forest that would come to be known as ecotourism. Today the free-spirited residents of Monteverde, three hours northwest of the capital, San José, are once again redefining responsible travel—yet now the goal extends beyond minimizing tourism’s footprint to actively restoring ecosystems, supporting local communities, and forging deeper connections between visitor and place. That ethos is embodied by Artista Villas, a collection of 10 swish bungalows in a reforestation site at Hotel Belmar. Guests at the carbon-neutral property, which opened in June, engage with the surrounding jungle using in-room art kits, meet visiting artists and filmmakers at the property’s Cervecería Belmar, forest bathe in the mountain at Artista-owned Savia nature reserve, and learn about the source of their meals at Finca Madre Tierra. Calling this new form of regenerative travel ecotourism feels too small to capture its weight.

Recent findings suggest that as conventional foreign-owned resorts proliferate along the nearby Gulf of Papagayo, Monteverde and the surrounding highlands continue to chart a different course. In March 2027 the working ranch and private reserve Hacienda Montezuma, located beneath the Tenorio Volcano (and normally reserved for exclusive buyouts), will launch the first in a series of wellness retreats bookable for up to 15 people. These will feature local practitioners leading equine therapy, meditation, and forest walks—all rooted in ancestral traditions. The region is also transitioning to a deforestation-free coffee model that is reshaping how one of Costa Rica's most key crops is both grown and experienced by visitors on educational tours. —Mark Johanson.

Go for: chef-led experiences, upcoming Cachapoal Valley bungalows, and up-and-coming wine scenes.

In a recent development, in Chile's best winemaking regions, there's plenty of old and new. Case in point: Chile’s most extravagant wine hotel, VIK, expanded in 2026 with eight glass-mirrored bungalows and an art-filled wellness center, with five cabins set to open next in an oak forest on the property.

Chile’s central wine valleys have long been defined by their vines—emerald rows sprawling along riverbanks, blanketing a terrain reminiscent of the Mediterranean, yet hemmed between towering Andes and a thrashing Pacific. Recently, dynamic chefs from Santiago have begun adding their touch to the region, crafting upcoming culinary tours and elevating the work of emerging bodegas and wineries. Kurt Schmidt is among them. He first rose to fame crafting nine-course tasting menus at Santiago’s 99 Restaurante, built around the traditional foodways of Chilean viticultural regions. In 2027 he’ll be teaming up with the rural tourism cooperative Ruta de los Abastos (“The Supply Route”) on menu-to-territory day tours that will begin at 99 and expand out to wine valleys like Huasco, Maule, and Aconcagua, where Schmidt has spent years building relationships with vintners, cheesemakers, foragers, and fisherfolk (later multiday itineraries are in the works). Conveniently, Santiago lies just south of the Maipo Valley, which is famed for bold Cabernet Sauvignons and also home to the striking new Centro del Vino from Concha y Toro, Latin America’s largest wine producer. The 129,000-square-foot facility features contemporary art installations, barrel-side tasting rooms, and an interactive wine museum, plus access to manicured gardens and (for an additional fee) the 19th-century mansion of founder Don Melchor.

It has been revealed that if you have days to spare, consider heading three hours south to the Cachapoal Valley. Here, Chile’s most extravagant wine hotel, VIK, expanded in 2026 with eight glass-mirrored bungalows and an art-filled wellness center. Five cabins are next, set to open in an oak forest on the property, where winemaker Cristián Vallejo ages natural wine in clay amphorae. Continuing south, you can explore the next generation of experimental and low-intervention vino emerging from the neighboring Maule and Itata valleys, where Millennial and Gen Z winemakers are injecting fresh energy into one of South America's oldest regions at bodegas like González Bastías and Carter Mollenhauer. Add it all up and it makes for an epic wine country road trip.

As if that weren’t enough to keep you busy, know that excellent vino isn’t the only reason to dedicate your big vacation to Chile this year. Once you wrap up in Santiago, consider hopping over to Rapa Nui (Easter Island) for some extreme set-jetting. This remote Chilean territory in the Southeastern Pacific is the backdrop of Academy Award winner Martin McDonagh’s new film, Wild Horse Nine, and it’s sure to become a rising star on more travelers’ itineraries this year. —Mark Johanson.

Go for: upcoming conservation-minded cruises, stargazing experiences, and an endless parade of wildlife.

In 2027 National Geographic–Lindblad Expeditions will celebrate 60 years since Lars-Eric Lindblad introduced travelers to the Galápagos on the first nonscientific civilian expedition voyage, establishing the islands as a premier destination for conservation-minded exploration.

The Galápagos Islands, an archipelago of 13 major isles and over 100 rocks and inlets off Ecuador’s coast, have long attracted travelers seeking solitude and wildlife: endemic giant tortoises and marine iguanas, native scalloped hammerhead sharks, and blue-footed boobies, for starters. Nearly 97% of the Galápagos’ land area is a single national park. Visitor access remains tightly managed, making the destination one of the rare places where travelers can experience wildlife on nature’s terms (and, as scientists are learning, occasionally encounter fresh species, like the deep-sea Microeledone galapagensis, or blue octopus). In 2027 National Geographic–Lindblad Expeditions will celebrate 60 years since Lars-Eric Lindblad introduced travelers to the Galápagos on the first nonscientific civilian expedition voyage, establishing the islands as a premier destination for conservation-minded exploration. The brand doubled its Galápagos fleet in 2025 by adding the 16-guest catamaran Delfina and the 48-guest Gemini. In January 2027 the brand will launch Ultimate Galápagos, a 13-day itinerary aboard the 96-passenger Endeavour II that visits 11 islands including remote Genovesa, known for its red-footed booby colonies. Elsewhere, Natural Habitat Adventures’ Galápagos Tortoise Camp just transitioned to 100% solar power and introduced the Galápagos’ first fully electric panga (a small skiff for excursions)—part of trips booked aboard the brand’s Petrel luxury catamaran—reducing emissions for wildlife excursions and setting a new benchmark for sustainable travel in the destination. —Hannah Selinger.

Go for: volcano trekking, peak birdwatching, price points that range from shoestring to major spender.

Guatemala, beloved for its artisan heritage, birdwatching, and volcano trekking up peaks like the Volcán de Fuego (pictured), will continue to draw a wide range of travelers in 2027.

Industry observers note that long a backpacking destination on the Central America 101 route known as the Gringo Trail, Guatemala is an increasingly popular destination for a generation of young travelers seeking slower, more enriching tourism that won’t break the bank. INGUAT, the Guatemala Institute of Tourism, says that arrival numbers support the TikTok thesis—and are only projected to increase. Some of the appeal is timeless: Guatemalan day-to-day life is deeply steeped in ancient heritage and culture. Sprawling artisan markets like Nim Po’t in Antigua offer easy access to hand-carved and painted wood animal masks, for example, but deeper dives are offered by Antigua-based textile studio Luna Zorro, which organizes craft retreats throughout the country. The brand’s recently opened La Valiente (February 2026) is a two-bedroom guesthouse in the heart of the city, and almost everything at the property—from the bedding to ceramics—is artisan-made by local creators. The country’s natural beauty is also an evergreen draw, but as younger generations embrace the mores—and aesthetics—of hiking (and even birdwatching), trails like the rigorous two-day Acatenango trek are list-toppers in the central highland region that is ripe with some of the 780 species recorded in Guatemala. Many choose to continue to the Tikal National Park in the northeast, where 3,000-year-old ruins of the Maya city sit amid a lush green jungle setting. At the park’s recently reopened Conservation and Research Center, visitors can observe the behind-the-scenes preservation process of ruins and artifacts, only now visible to the public. It all makes for welcome news that Guatemala is getting even easier to access: Frontier is offering daily, seasonal, nonstop service from Los Angeles to Guatemala City from December 17 until January 4, if you need a last-minute holiday getaway, and United Airlines has a permanent direct route from Houston. —Anna Zou.

Go for: untamed rainforest, immersive eco-lodges, and easier-than-ever access.

Guyana still remains 85% forested, with sites like the impressive Kaieteur Falls—among the world's strongest single-drop waterfalls—awaiting travelers.

Industry observers note that guyana, South America’s only country with English as its official language, celebrated six decades of nationhood this May. Yet from a small plane bound for Kaieteur Falls, one of the most powerful single-drop waterfalls in the world, the lush rainforest below appears several geological eras older. Perhaps it’s no wonder; an impressive 85% of this country remains forested.

Most travelers start in the coastal city of Georgetown, where the country’s Caribbean identity is tangible in the annual Mashramani carnival (every February), vibrant Stabroek Market, and Gothic St. George’s Anglican Cathedral, which is made of wood. But journeys rapidly turn toward the rainforest and savanna, with Kaieteur as their most dramatic introduction. At the falls, the Potaro River drops 741 feet from a sandstone ledge—more than four times Niagara’s height—yet just over 8,000 people see it each year, usually on a day flight from Georgetown. A fuller interior journey requires a separate, multiday circuit through Iwokrama International Centre for Rainforest Conservation and Development (IIC), a nearly million-acre reserve managed alongside 20 Indigenous communities, and into the North Rupununi, a landscape of savanna, wetlands, and river villages where Indigenous-led conservation becomes part of the itinerary. For in-the-know travelers, right now—when a host of newly introduced expeditions and accommodations have risen to meet vanguard voyage interest—is the time to go.

According to recent reports, on that circuit, three conservation-linked stays give travelers a direct role in the work. Atta Rainforest Lodge is the base for Iwokrama’s canopy walkway, suspended 100 feet above the forest floor and managed by the reserve in partnership with Makushi communities and local tourism operators. Further into the North Rupununi, road and river lead to Rewa Eco-Lodge, operated by Rewa Village, where anglers help measure and tag arapaima before release. Another tributary leads to Yupukari’s Caiman House, a village-run guesthouse and research station where visitors help researchers study black caiman after dark. The community also raises yellow-spotted Amazon river turtles for release. Reaching these stays still requires small planes and long road-and-river transfers, though one notable link is easing: In August 2026, Jags Aviation added a 19-seat turboprop service four days a week between Georgetown’s Eugene F. Correia International Airport and Lethem.

In a recent development, back in Georgetown, the arrival of international hotel brands marks a newly introduced era at the start and finish of any trip. The 152-room AC Hotel opened in December 2025, with the 172-room Four Points by Sheraton following in April 2026. A Hilton resort is due on the seafront in 2028. And there are more reasons to linger in 2027: From October 8 to October 17, the capital will also host Carifesta XVI, which will return the Caribbean Festival of Arts to its 1972 birthplace, promising a cultural counterpart to the wilderness of the interior. —Paul Jebara.

Go for: fresh off-season expeditions, and a slate of fresh lodges.

For the first time in 2026, tour manufacturer Hielo & Aventura offered its popular ice hiking excursion atop the Perito Moreno Glacier—in winter.

It has been revealed that los Glaciares National Park, with its toothy granite spires, windswept steppe, and glaciers that crack and roar as they calve into milky-blue lakes, has long been the crown jewel of Argentine Patagonia. Yet its main gateway town, El Calafate, hasn’t seen a fresh luxury hotel in over two decades. That changes in December 2026 with Explora El Calafate, an all-inclusive 20-key lodge snaking across a Patagonian estancia near Lake Argentino. The hotel’s design leans into soothing earth tones—with giant windows framing distant glaciers—while menus highlight Patagonian lamb, trout, and wine. Guides take guests on 30 different adventures out to remote wildlands like the ice fields of Brazo Sur or the bird sanctuary of Laguna Nimez. Explora will simultaneously open a second property just across the Chilean border in its private Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve, further linking the two destinations by building out a binational circuit.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, southern Patagonia is shedding its reputation as a summer-only destination. Awasi Patagonia, near Torres del Paine, will now remain open through the 2027 winter season—prime time for puma safaris—while ecotourism operator Chile Nativo extols the virtue of the offseason with its Winter W Trek, tracing the iconic route past Paine Grande and the Grey Glacier in the region’s quieter season. The momentum is even greater in Los Glaciares. In 2026 park concessionaire Hielo & Aventura, responding to greater off-season demand that can help disperse the annual tourist traffic, operated its popular ice hiking excursion atop the Perito Moreno Glacier during the winter for the first time. Unlike most Patagonian mountain towns, El Calafate doesn’t shut down when crowds depart, which means there are still hot chocolates to be had after a day on the ice. —Mark Johanson.

Go for: a buyout villa in jaguar country, and groundbreaking conservation efforts.

Caiman’s newly introduced private villa, Cordilheira, has seven bungalows with buyout options for larger groups, offering a new way to stay in this wildlife-rich corner of Brazil.

It has been revealed that for flora and fauna lovers headed to South America, the Amazon has long been the marquee trip. But further south, where the waters of the Amazon trickle down into the world’s largest tropical wetland, something different awaits. The Pantanal stretches across 42 million acres in Brazil, Bolivia, and Paraguay. In comparison to the Amazon, it’s a bit more arid, with strong cowboy culture, and the foliage is sparser, making this a great place to spot jaguars in the wild. This is in no small part thanks to crucial conservation work that has taken place over decades. At the upscale Caiman Pantanal, a trailblazing safari stay in the Brazilian Pantanal, jaguar rescue group Onçafari has an on-site location, allowing guests at the all-inclusive property to explore 131,000 acres of land with the substantial cat experts who have meticulously tagged and tracked dozens of them. Caiman’s upcoming private villa, Cordilheira, was unveiled in June 2026. It brings together seven bungalows (private infinity pools included) that fit up to 16 people, making it possible for families and groups to have a buyout experience as they spend days tracking jaguars—and tapirs, and giant anteaters, and capybaras—before evenings filled with Brazilian barbecue and folk music under the stars. Operators like Natural Habitat Adventures can continue the journey northbound to destinations like Porto Jofre, where cat sightings happen by boat on the river, and jaguars can be seen chasing caimans at the water’s edge. The conservation work required to protect this rare natural landscape and its fauna is ongoing, but new projects like the Jaguar Rivers Initiative, announced in fall 2025, prove the only way is forward. This new coalition, which connects the aforementioned Onçafari with Kristine Tompkins’s Fundación Rewilding Argentina, Nativa in Bolivia, and Fundación Moisés Bertoni in Paraguay, hopes to better link and restore various jaguar habitats. The goal is, of course, ecological first and foremost—but if the preservation work in Pantanal has taught us anything so far, it’s that great conservation can lead to great wildlife experiences. —Megan Spurrell.

Go for: uncrowded surf spots, a noteworthy beach hideaway, and plenty of seafood.

Opened in February 2026, resort Inkaterra Cabo Blanco overlooks the Pacific Ocean on a coastline frequented by Marilyn Monroe and Ernest Hemingway.

The seaside towns and villages of Peru's northern shore are known for their seafood dishes, such as picante de mariscos and raw-fish tiraditos.

According to recent reports, on Peru’s northern coast, life moves slowly in the seaside towns and fishing villages that have long drawn a quiet trickle of visitors including surfers chasing mythical waves, Limeños lured by closer-to-the-equator sun and tranquility, and culinary-minded travelers who know that nowhere else does seafood quite like this part of the country. In the past few years, an increasingly stylish crop of Airbnbs have popped up—like Kahu Beach House in Los Órganos, where modern design uses endemic natural materials and where fantastic surf breaks are visible from your breakfast table. The more recent resort opening of Inkaterra Cabo Blanco in February 2026 has shone an even brighter spotlight: On the same stretch of sand where Marilyn Monroe and Ernest Hemingway vacationed in the 1950s, this contemporary beachside stay with just 13 rooms is an elegant approach to the destination’s barefoot ease, refined coastal dining, and experiences that range from a day on the water with a local fishing collective to surfing and kitesurfing lessons just steps from the private plunge pools. As for the region’s culinary offerings? You won’t have to look hard. This sun-baked stretch of coast is where carne seca dries on clotheslines and makes its way into seco de chavela (a pounded beef and plantain dish bursting with chile), and where Peruvian classics like conchas a la parmesana (scallops baked with cheese) are remixed using conchas negras, a unique shellfish found in the mangroves of Tumbes, near the border with Ecuador. Hearty dishes like picante de mariscos, a seafood stew, sit side by side with chilled raw-fish tiraditos that fly close to the sun in their spice. —Megan Spurrell.

Go for: kitesurfing for pros—and newbies—in a fishing village now home to quietly luxurious stays.

With the charm of a fishing village and powerful winds, Preá has become an ideal kitesurfing destination.

From spa treatments to horseback riding and yoga Preá's hotel scene brings a bevy of activities to travelers.

Industry observers note that preá has the unmistakable charm of a Brazilian fishing village—a seemingly endless shoreline, a sandy-street village center, and beachfront restaurants serving fresh-caught seafood—with one major difference: wind, and lots of it. From July through early January, this sleepy town catches some of the world’s most consistently powerful gusts, the kind kitesurfers cross oceans for. Now, with the sport growing in popularity, beginners are starting to come too, bringing with them an exciting latest energy. Kitesurfing has become so popular among Brazil’s well-heeled travelers that Marco Dalpozzo, a partner at the pioneering pousada Rancho do Peixe, dubbed the sport “the new golf, the new tennis, the new skiing.” Learning takes some commitment: First-timers start on the sand before progressing into the water, with a full beginner course happening over several days. Yet new kitesurfing locations are making it easier than ever for newcomers to join the scene.

It has been revealed that while the famed Jericoacoara next door is known for its lively nightlife and parties, Preá’s latest crop of high-end boutique hotels and villas offers a more exclusive take on barefoot luxury. Think ocean-facing rooms, intimate private villas, and seaside bungalows paired with their own kite schools, full-service spas, and feet-in-the-sand restaurants. Whether you’re up for braving the wind or not, there is plenty else to do in terms of both adventure and restorative wellness.

According to recent reports, preá offers easy access to the landscapes that made neighboring Jericoacoara famous. Set off by buggy or quad to explore the region’s enormous sand dunes and freshwater lagoons that naturally occur between them, or visit the otherworldly Jericoacoara National Park. Back in Preá, book a treatment at L’Occitane spa at the Preabeach Boutique Hotel, take advantage of the yoga offerings at Hotel Kabana, or horseback ride along the shore. By sunset, everyone gathers on the beach to watch the last kiters streak across the water as what looks like a giant ball of fire slips into the ocean. Later, dinner can range from candlelit seaside dining to charming restaurants like Casinha in the rustic village center, where flip-flops are acceptable attire.

The wind is bringing in major investments too. Grupo Carnaúba is building what it envisions as the wind sports equivalent to an Alpine ski resort. Its members-only Carnaúba Wind House, opened in 2024, offers bungalow stays with a kite center, beach club, restaurant, and freshwater lagoon, while the larger Vila Carnaúba development is adding more luxury residences and beach tennis facilities. The biggest arrival yet comes in 2028, when Anantara opens its first property in the Americas: A beachfront resort complete with its own signature spa and dedicated kitesurfing school. —Carla Vianna.

Go for: cheffy restaurant openings, a revitalized downtown, and a lineup of literary festivals.

Bachour by Mata (above) is pastry chef Antonio Bachour's first Latin American pastry shop—and it joins a wave of buzzy culinary openings that have made this city an increasingly hot food destination.

Sources indicate that são Paulo is a city for those with an appetite—for business, culture, and, of course, food. Brazil’s largest and most frenetic metropolis is home to some of Brazil’s most extraordinary architectural landmarks, from Lina Bo Bardi’s museum of art (MASP) to Paulo Mendes da Rocha’s reimagined Pinacoteca do Estado de São Paulo. Meanwhile, the restaurant landscape has never been more exciting: São Paulo is now home to the only two restaurants in the Southern Hemisphere recently awarded three Michelin stars: Tuju and Evvai.

That momentum is reshaping the city well beyond its established dining districts: Near Avenida Paulista, the Mata São Paulo hospitality complex has gathered some of the city’s buzziest names, including Mata Città, Korean barbecue spot Lavva, and pastry chef Antonio Bachour, who opened his first Latin American pastry shop Bachour by Mata here, all in one place. More is on the way, including a fresh boteco, Á Brasileira, from Janaína Torres (named the World’s Best Female Chef in 2024 by World’s 50 Best). Her beloved Bar da Dona Onça, on the ground floor of Oscar Niemeyer’s sinuous Copan building, has itself gained new neighbors, including seafood-focused Brisa do Barú and Tem Umami!, an ice cream shop with a near-permanent line out the door. Together with an observation deck, the new arrivals are turning the 1,160-apartment Modernist landmark into one of downtown’s liveliest destinations.

Also inside the Copan is Livraria Megafauna, part of a new wave of independent bookstores bringing literary life back to São Paulo’s streets. Its Poesia no Centro poetry festival, returning in April 2027, has already become a fixture on the city’s cultural calendar; meanwhile the growing Feira do Livro, organized by literary magazine Quatro Cinco Um, is expected to draw around 100,000 people to the Praça Charles Miller in May 2027, and it will nearly double the space devoted to its mostly independent publishers.

According to recent reports, that literary boom is part of a broader cultural surge, with major events like SP-Arte in April and the Bienal de São Paulo—Latin America’s largest visual arts event—returning to Ibirapuera Park in September. The expansion of Museu de Arte de São Paulo Assis Chateaubriand, the city’s landmark art museum, only adds to the momentum: Its newest building, opened in March 2025, increased exhibition space by more than 60% and made room for latest highlights and works from the collection previously kept out of public view. —Rafael Tonon.

Tech Report: Finding Unexpected Joy In Music And Hospitality From Los Angeles To Malibu

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (533 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Liveandletsfly

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that one of the beautiful things about traveling around the world is the chance to experience hospitality in different ways in different countries.
  • I listen to music during the day as I work on this blog and on my other work.
  • As I listened to her music all morning, one of her YouTube shorts noted that she would be performing a classical concert in Los Angeles, which immediately piqued my interest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that one of the beautiful things about traveling around the world is the chance to experience hospitality in different ways in different countries. I’ll never forget the hospitality I experienced In Iran or in Ukraine, but sometimes we don’t have to travel far to experience it, as I recently found out in Los Angeles.

I listen to music during the day as I work on this blog and on my other work. Some people require absolute silence to work, but I like music, specially Christian hymns. I primarily use YouTube and of course the algorithm gets to know you. There’s no music I like more than a powerful organ playing a beloved hymn. Lately, the algorithm has been suggesting a very gifted organist named Lauma Akmene, a Latvian-born musician who is the organist, conductor, and music director at St. Peter’s Episcopal Church in Salisbury, Maryland.

As I listened to her music all morning, one of her YouTube shorts noted that she would be performing a classical concert in Los Angeles, which immediately piqued my interest.

Industry observers note that I obtained a ticket and found the concert would be held at a place called Stan’s Musical Parlor, which was actually a beautiful 1926 home in LA’s posh Lafayette Square neighborhood. Not knowing quite what to expect, I highlighted up and was warmly greeted by Stanley Harris himself, who I came to find out has opened his house since 1986 to showcase musical talents. Dr. Harris is a retired psychiatrist and was a longtime clinician and faculty member at the University of Southern California.

Industry observers note that stan has a Johannus-BachMen-Hauptwerk organ (including Hauptwerk virtual pipe organs) in his living room. Essentially, this digital organ can be set to emulate sounds from many of famous pipe organs around the world.

The concert began at 8:00 pm and was simply fabulous, with Lauma playing several classic and neo-classic works.

One of the guests mentioned that he was hosting Lauma the following evening at his home in Malibu, and invited me to attend. I had to be in Palm Springs for work that day, but I drove from Palms Springs all the way to Malibu via Pacific Coast Highway (took about three hours!) and made it just in time for the concert, another fabulous evening of food, fellowship, and great music.

Already, I’ve made friends through these two events, who I am staying in touch with, and will go to more of these concerts. Community is beautiful thing, as is hospitality, and all in my backyard, one of the many reasons I love Los Angeles and Southern California so much.

Truth be told, I almost did not go to either event. I was tired and probably could have used a couple extra hours of sleep. But I’m so glad I did go and I’m thankful to YouTube for suggesting Lauma and making these two possible in the first place.

Lauma is such a gifted organist. If you like classical music and especially sacred music, you can enjoy her work here.

According to recent reports, join our mailing list for a daily summary of posts! We never sell your info.

Check your offer: Save up to 50% on Amazon purchases using just 429 Amex points

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thepointsguy

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whether you’re stocking up on household staples or preparing for Black Friday deals to tackle your holiday shopping, there are many ways to save on Amazon orders.
  • And if you have an American Express card that earns American Express Membership Rewards points, you may be eligible for a newly introduced offer that can help you save up to 50% on Amazon purchases.
  • Related: TPG's guide to Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whether you’re stocking up on household staples or preparing for Black Friday deals to tackle your holiday shopping, there are many ways to save on Amazon orders.

And if you have an American Express card that earns American Express Membership Rewards points, you may be eligible for a newly introduced offer that can help you save up to 50% on Amazon purchases.

Related: TPG's guide to Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals.

Typically, using Membership Rewards points for Amazon purchases isn’t a great option, as the value per point is below that of most travel redemptions. However, right now, you can save as much as 50% on an Amazon purchase by cashing in as few as 429 Membership Rewards points with some current targeted offers.

Other cards also have Amazon offers right now.

Some TPG staffers received offers as high as 50% (up to $50), which is one of the highest we've ever seen.

Others had smaller offers of 15% off (or none at all).

Recent findings suggest that the requirement to spend at least 429 Membership Rewards points is better than many of the times we've seen this offer. Back in November 2025, the requirement was 714 points, but previously it had been as low as 1 point.

In a recent development, remember that these are targeted offers, so they will vary. Hopefully, you are targeted for the larger offers.
